maintopic: CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE

speechtext: On motion of Mr. J. J. Denis (Joliette) the second and final report of the select standing committee on privileges and elections was concurred in.

subtopic: NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Hon. J. II. KING (Minister of Health) moved:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this house agrees to their amendments to clauses 4, 5 subsection 4 (1), 5 subsection 4 (3) inserted, 24, 29, 32 subsection 6 and new clause A, and disagrees to their amendments to clauses 2 (a), 7, 12, 25, 30, (10), and 31 to bill No. 289, an act to amend the Pension Act, for the following reasons:
Because in respect of clause 30, subsection 10, the amendments made by the Senate differ in form and substance from those made by them to clause 5, subsection 4 (1) and are likely to cause confusion and misunderstanding in their interpretation. There is no objection to requiring the approval of the commission or of the board before the payment of accounts, but the right to question expenditure must lie with the minister who is responsible to parliament for the proper use of the moneys with which he is entrusted.
This safeguard is implied in subsection 4 (1) of clause 5 as amended by the Senate in the provision that the commission shall be attached to the department. There is no such safeguard provided in the amendment by the Senate to subsection 10 of clause . 30. The board should not possess a greater control of expenditure than that given to the commission. It is considered that the situation would be clarified and the two bodies placed upon an equal footing in this respect if an amendment similar to that made to subsection 4 (1) of clause 5, were made to subsection (10) of clause 30. The subsection would then read as follows:
"The board shall be attached to the department and the expenses required to be incurred

Pension Act-Senate Amendments
for the discharge of its duties, including the salaries of its officers, clerks, and other employees shall, on approval by the board, be paid, out of the moneys provided by parliament."
Because in respect of clause 12, while this house concurs in the amendments made by the Senate as to the special tribunal that is to consider cases claimed to be specially meritorious it is not clear what course must be followed by the applicant before he presents his application to such special tribunal. The term "entitlement" as used in the amendments made by the Senate is not defined by the Pension Act. There are several cases which might properly be made the subject of an award of a compassionate pension or allowance which are obviously not pensionable as a matter of right under the Pension Act. If it is intended that before applications are made to the special tribunal, the applicant must first apply to the commission in all cases, even if obviously not provided for in the Pension Act, and must make a further application to the board only in those cases, where, under the Pension Act, an appeal lies to the board, it is considered that such intention would be made clear by deleting the words "and in which entitlement has been refused by the commission, and by the board where the right of appeal exists" as contained in the amendments made by the Senate and substituting therefor "and in which pension has been refused by the commission, or if an appeal lies to the board, both by the commission and by the board
Because in respect of clauses 2 (a), 7, 25 and 31, this house adopted these clauses unanimously. They were based upon the report of the special committee of this house on pensions and returned soldiers' problems, who were unanimous in their findings and recommendations. The said committee held forty-seven sessions and heard representatives of various soldier organizations throughout Canada, departmental officers, the chairman and officials both of the commission and of the board. The report of the special committee was concurred in unanimously hy this house. The clauses are designed to remove grievances which the special committee considered well founded and to extend the payment of pensions to persons who ought to be entitled thereto. The amendments to these clauses made by the Senate are considered to be not in the public interest.
Because in respect of clause 7, under the provisions of section 11a of the Pension Act, although pension is paid to a member of the forces in respect of the aggravation of an injury or disease existing prior to enlistment resulting in disability where such aggravation was attributable to or was incurred during military service, yet no pension is payable to the dependents of such member of the forces on his death unless it is proved to the commission that such aggravation was itself the cause of his death, the object of this house in passing clause 7 was to provide for the payment of pensions to the dependents of such member of the forces on his death where the aggravation although not itself the cause of his death was a substantial factor in causing it. The clause is easier of application than the present law and would give a greater latitude to the commission to award pensions in accordance with the fundamental principle of the Pension Act that a pension shall be paid to the dependents
of a deceased member of the forces if the death of such member took place during or was attributable to his military service.
Because in respect of clause 25 it is considered that the provisions of section 32 of the Pension Act, that no pension shall be paid to the widow of a member of the forces unless she was married to him before the appearance of the injury or disease which resulted in his death, are too wide in their extent. While it is in the public interest not to pay a pension to a woman who married a member of the forces in the expectation that she would receive a pension upon his death, it is not in the public interest or just that pensions should be denied to all widows who come within the class described in section 32. Nor is it in the public interest that members of the forces who have suffered disability by reason of military service should be in a different position as regards marriage from other members of the forces. The object of this house in passing clause 25 was to provide pensions in deserving cases, at the same time providing necessary safeguards. It is considered that difficulties of interpretation and application might be overcome by providing that a pension shall be paid to the widow of a member of the forces, notwithstanding her marriage to him after the appearance of the injury or disease which resulted in his death, provided that such marriage took place prior to the coming into force of the Pension Act of 1919, or that at the time of such marriage the member of the forces was not over forty years of age, was not in receipt of a pension in respect of the injury or disease which resulted in his death, and was not seriously ill.
Because in respect of clause 2a, which defines the term "appearance of the injury or disease" as the same is used in section 32 of the Pension Act, it is considered that the provisions of the said section ought not to extend to the widow of a member of the forces who was married to him after the appearance of an injury or disease and after such injury or disease had been reduced sufficiently to permit him to serve in a theatre of actual war, provided the marriage was prior to the recurrence of such injury or disease.
Because in respect of clause 31 under the provisions of section 51 of the Pension Act the only question on which an appeal lies from the decision of the commission is as to whether the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death was attributable to or incurred during military service. The object of this house in passing clause 31 was to widen the scope of appeal. It is in the public interest that the returned soldiers and their dependents should have confidence in the administration of the Pension Act, and this object would have been accomplished by providing for a review by the board of decisions of the commission where applicants felt themselves aggrieved. It is considered that an appeal should lie to the board on decisions made, for example, under the provisions of sections 12, 30, 32, 33, 34 and 39 of the Pension Act. Clause 30 would have provided an appeal and an opportunity of correcting error, subject to the proviso therein contained, on such questions. By reason of the amendments by the Senate no such appeal is allowed.
And that the Clerk do carry the said message to the Senate.
3726	COMMONS
Pension Act-Senate Amendments
He said:	In moving that we disagree with,
the Senate amendments referred to I wish to say that a great deal of consideration was given the amendments to the Pension Act by a special committee of this house, who unanimously reported in favour of the bill which was presented to this house, and adopted unanimously by the house. The matter is one which deals with a great social problem of the Canadian people, the care of the men and the dependents of the men who served overseas. There has been at all times a desire among the Canadian people to do full justice to the returned soldiers and their dependents, who served the Canadian people during the war overseas. This bill was sent to the Senate and has 'been returned to this house with certain amendments; certain sections considered important by the House of Commons have been deleted. We think the matter of sufficient importance to disagree with these changes, and I therefore move that this message be sent to the Senate in order that they may have an opportunity of reconsidering the sections which they have deleted and the other changes they have made.

subtopic: NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I wish to say only a word or two regarding this motion, referring to the particular clause which asks the Senate to reconsider its decision with respect to widows who had married ex-soldiers after the appearance of disability. The underlying principle laid down by those who first looked after pension legislation was that any woman who married a soldier after he had been injured or had incurred illness on service, would not upon his death be entitled to a pension. This clause has been considered too restricted and committees of the House of Commons, and the house itself, have on four separate occasions passed legislation to amend the act with respect to this very deserving class of widows.
This year the committee brought in a unanimous report which was concurred in unanimously by the house, and when the discussion took place in this chamber there was no difference of opinion on the principle. The amendment of the committee apparently did not satisfy the members of the Senate, who stated that it was unworkable and that it was perhaps too broad. However, for the first time, I learn that members of the Senate have agreed in principle that, with proper safeguards, the widow who in good faith married a member of the forces who returned from overseas suffering from an injury or disease contracted on service should receive a pension. There is no difference of opinion with regard to the principle, and it seems to

me that if the Senate and the House of Commons have agreed in principle, surely we should be able to find some formula or phraseology which will give a pension to this most deserving class of people. That is the situation as it stands to-day. I freely admit, as chairman of the committee, that fault might be found with the amendment which was sent up to the committee, but I am not prepared to agree that it was altogether unworkable, nor am I prepared to agree that it was too broad. If an injustice is being done a certain class of persons in this country, it is preposterous to go to the country and say we know the injustice is being done but the united wisdom of the House of Commons and of the Senate is incapable of formulating a provision to rectify it.
We have had informal conferences-perhaps they were not constitutional-at which members of the committee, the Minister of Pensions and Health, the Minister of National Defence and members of the house have appeared before the Senate committee. Due to the emphatic and blunt pronouncement of my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Ross) we were able to save one clause from the wreck, that which did away with the limitation of time for making application for pension.
If this house is unanimously of the opinion that a clause should be inserted in the bill to provide for this class of people, we should be able to say to the house, with the assistance of the officers of the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment, that the members of the committee on pensions are prepared to make any suggestion and to discuss the whole question with the members of the Senate or of the Senate committee. More than that, any member of the house who knows the Pension Act is prepared to offer his services. The leader of the opposition, a gentleman of high legal standing, and, may I say without irony, a master of phraseology and a moulder of words, would I am sure be only too glad to join with members on the other side of the house to discuss this question with the members of the Senate in an effort to find a solution of the difficulty.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	I have
just one word to say before this motion is allowed to pass. It has been my privilege in the past to be chairman of a committee similar to the one that was sitting this year, and it is needless for me to say that I am in entire sympathy with the desire to give due recognition to the rights and privileges of the soldiers; I want every returned man and his family to receive the pension to

which they are entitled. On the other hand, I am against what you might call the speculators; the country must be very careful to see that this class of people are not included in the amendments passed each year.
It must be remembered that in the United States after the civil war a very serious state of affairs developed. I will not go into details because the facts are well known to everyone. I might however point out that at present the amount that the country is paying for pensions to returned soldiers and their dependents is several million dollars more that it was, say, five years after the war was over. One would imagine that ten years after t'he conclusion of the war the amount paid for pensions should begin to decrease; but it is not decreasing, it is increasing every year. I have not the exact figures under my hand but I know them practically by heart. About five, six or seven years ago we were paying $31,000,000, $32,000,000, $33,000,000 a year, whereas now we are paying $40,000,000 a year. Therefore I think parliament should be very careful in the passing of legislation all the time enlarging the number of pensioners. No doubt it is on that principle that the senate rejected part of the bill that was passed by the Commons. In resuming my seat I wish to repeat once more that I am in entire sympathy with returned men and I want them to receive all the good the country can give them, but I am not in sympathy with those who may, under cover of being dependents of returned men, be preying on the country's generosity.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:

Bill reported, read the third time and passed.	'

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital -Hudson Bay railway and terminals: construction and betterments, including E. B. Jost at $2,500, $6,500,000.

Will the minister give an explanation of this appropriation?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): Perhaps a brief statement regarding the progress being made and what is contemplated in the current fiscal year would be advisable at this stage. In 1926, as the committee will remember, the Hudson Bay railway consisted of 332 miles of railway which had been constructed ten to fifteen yeans previously and which had gone completely out of condition. The original ties on the road were all of native spruce and they had all rotted in the intervening period. A large proportion of the construction being over muskeg country, the embankment had gone very badly out of condition. The telegraph line was completely destroyed. There were no water facilities and no engine terminal facilities at any point on the line.
It will be remembered that at the session of 1926 provision was made in the estimates for the rehabilitation of the existing line of railway. That work has since proceeded and it is now well toward completion. Engine terminal facilities have been provided at the commencement of the line at Le Pas and at mile 137, and another engine terminal is now under construction at mile 327. In addition steel has been laid beyond mile 332 to mile 356, whidh is the present end of steel, six miles beyond the Limestone river. It will be remembered that last year there was placed in the estimates a further appropriation to complete the reconditioning of the existing track and at the same time an intimation was given to the house that an investigation would be conducted during 1927 regarding the matter of ocean terminals. That investigation, as was announced in the house last session, was conducted by Mr. Frederick Palmer, president of the British Institution of Civil Engineers. I had the privilege of accompanying Mr. Palmer on the journey to Hudson bay. He and his assistant also spent some time here on the first trip to this country, going through all the records of the department in relation to the whole enterprise, and coming bach again in the month of July and early August to make an actual inspection of Nelson and Churchill on the ground. As a result of that work, Mr. Palmer reported very emphatically in favour of making the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway, Churchill, rather than Nelson. His report was published by the government immediately and was given very wide circulation. I think every member of the house received at least one copy of it, and a number of members more than one, and therein are set out the economic reasons for the recommendations made.

Supply-Hudson Bay Railway
Briefly I can summarize them by saying that there is no question in the mind of Mr. Palmer or of any of the Canadian engineers who ao-oompanied the party that Churchill can be more cheaply, more economically developed into a safer port than Nelson. If in the subsequent discussion further information is desired than that brief statement, which I think a careful reading of the report on the part of any member will confirm, I shall be glad to give the information.
With regard to the extension, of the railway to Churchill, the construction work is in the hands of the Canadian National Railways in the same manner as the reconstruction of the original track. The Canadian National has let the contract for the grading of the last piece of line from the present end of steel to Churchill.
The vote asked for this year is $6,500,000, of which $3,500,000 is for railway purposes and $3,000,000 for port development. It will be understood that in making arrangements for the construction of the port a large portion of the initial expenditure must necessarily be on equipment to do the work. I may say that every effort was made to get ready for active construction work at the port during the fall and winter of 1927. Immediate instructions were given, following the confirmation by the government of Churchill as the terminus, to have the dredge Kennequ-hair which was built many years ago for Hudson bay service', and which was then at Halifax, transferred to Churchill during the fall of 1927, the idea being that if a dredge could be placed at Churchill during 1927 it would be immediately available for work in the season of 1928. Hon. members will understand the difficulty of attempting, with our present knowledge of navigation conditions, to get into the bay before the month of July, it is not practical to expect that a dredge shipped into Churchill in the month of July or August could accomplish very much in the way of dredging work in the season during which she travels from the Nova Scotia coast to Churchill. Unfortunately, although the Kennequhair was sent to Churchill, it was necessaiy, in a storm in the north Atlantic, in order to save the lives of the crew of the tug and the crew of the dredge, for the tug to cut the hawser after three days of very stormy weather, and consequently the Kennequhair was lost. That has rendered it necessary to provide new dredging equipment, and in all probability that will involve some delay in the completion of the dredging work at Churchill. Every effort is being made by the department to speed up the work consistent with the necessary provisions for safety. It

is not an easy task to construct a great engineering enterprise so far from our normal business and industrial bases, and particularly is that the case with respect to floating equipment, because it must of necessity be sent in by sea, and there is the limitation of the navigation conditions ais we presently know them in that regard.
The department conducted an investigation into the loss of the Kennequhair, and we cannot attribute blame to any individual with respect thereto. The loss was incurred not in the straits or in the bay, but in the waters of the north Atlantic. There was, if my memory of the report serves me aright, a continuous storm for three days. The dredge was being towed by the tug on a hawser, a leak developed and this gradually increased until on the third night it was not deemed safe to allow the crew to remain on the dredge. Consequently, when it became dark, those members of the crew who were on the dredge were transferred by orders of the navigator to the tug for their safety, and during the night it became necessary to cut the hawser and let the dredge go. She sank immediately. These are things, of course, which we must expect occasionally in attempting enterprises of this character. Wie hope for better luck in the future.
During the winter arrangements were made to transfer as much as possible of the useful equipment at Nelson to Churchill. For that purpose Lynn tractors, commonly used in large lumbering enterprises, were employed, and a large amount of useful material has been transferred overland from Nelson to Churchill in order that it may be available during the coming summer. Hon. members who are familiar with the sea will understand that the first job to do this summer is to arrange for some landing facilities at Churchill, some temporary pier construction in order that the vessels arriving there may unload economically instead of having to transfer in deep water to smaller boats or scows. The material is being assembled for that purpose, and it is proposed this year to send in approximately 13,500 tons of material by sea. It is hoped by the time the material reaches Churchill that the force now there, with the material now there, will have a temporary pier constructed in such a manner as to enable all material to be unloaded in the most economical fashion.
That is all I have in mind at the moment. I expect a number of inquiries, and shall endeavour to give as much further detail o" the committee may desire.

Supply-Hudson Bay Railway

Would the minister be
good enough to repeat at what point the dredge was lost?

I have not the exact
latitude and longitude, but it was in the north Atlantic, a considerable distance off the Labrador coast.

How many
miles is it from the end of steel to Churchill, and what is the estimated cost to complete the line to Churchill? Secondly, how far would it be from that line when completed to Nelson? The line was originally intended to run to Nelson, but has been diverted to Churchill. Does the government contemplate building a line to Nelson from the main line running to Churchill?

I am just looking up
the exact figures which are contained in Mr. Palmer's report. These were all carefully checked, and I prefer to use them rather than to rely on my memory. The diversion to Churchill occurs at a point seventy miles from Nelson, the line turning north at that point to Churchill.
That would be the nearest point on the line to Nelson?

Yes, that is mile 356
from Le Pas, where the northward turn occurs. From that point it is 154 miles to Churchill and 68 miles to Nelson.
What is the estimated cost of completion of the line to Churchill?

The extra capital cost
over and above what it would cost to build the line to Nelson is what my hon. friend is asking for?
No.

I will give that figure
first; it has a bearing on the other. It will cost $5,085,000 more to build the line to Churchill than to Nelson. These are the figures of the Canadian National engineers. The total cost-I am sorry I cannot put my finger on this figure just now.

If you had
the cost to Port Nelson you could figure it out.
Yes. It is between seven and eight million dollars, but I prefer to be absolutely accurate.

The other
part of my question was:	Does the government contemplate building the sixty-eight miles from that point to Nelson, as well as the line on to Churchill?
Not at the present time. Whatever may eventuate in the future we cannot foresee. If my hon. friend will read the whole engineering report with respect to the two places-
I have-

It is possible. With the great development taking place in the northland at the present time, he would be a bold man indeed who would venture to state definitely that the line never would be built to Nelson. In view of the remarkable occurrences now taking place in that part of Canada, I prefer not to commit myself to stating that the line to Nelson will never be built. It may be, but for the present we cannot see any immediate necessity for it. Now I have the figures for my hon. friend. The railway to Nelson would cost $2,458,000, that is, from the point of junction, the cost of the railway to Churchill would be $7,543,000, the difference between the two being the figure I previously gave.
# Mr. IRVINE: Some months ago, Mr. Chairman, I noticed in the press a report to the effect that the government had taken steps to prevent speculation in real estate at the new port of Churchill. If the report is correct, I wish to congratulate the minister and the government. I think we all agree that the real estate speculation which has characterized the development of town sites in the west is something which is not healthy and, if preventable, it would be a great advantage to the general public. If the report is substantially correct, I desire to ask the minister what steps he proposes to take. I should like to know also if he is making an experiment with respect to this particular townsite-I think the time is ripe for it- which would prevent all such speculation as in the past took place in the west.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I
can indicate to the committee the steps taken up to now. Immediately on the selection of Churchill as .the Hudson bay port one of the problems the department had to meet was with respect to the land ownership there. There was a certain amount of land on the west peninsula-on which most of the works will be situated-which had been owned by private parties for many years. The great bulk of the land was still in the crown under the Department of the Interior. I felt that

Supply-Hudson Bay Railway

considerable difficulty might arise, especially due to the fact that a large portion of the privately owned land was distant more than four miles from the point at which the port works would be situated. I may say frankly to my hon. friend that I visioned all sorts of possibilities of enterprising individuals offering lots for sale at Churchill which the unfortunate purchasers, later would find were approximately four miles from the port itself, and with the resultant trouble which always follows that sort of thing.
As in a lot of western towns.

Yes. It was deemed
wise-the government accepted my recommendation in that regard-to expropriate all the privately owned property on the east peninsula at Churchill, and the present situation is that no private individuals own any property there. The Hudson's Bay Company has a certain area reserved on the west peninsula, on the other side of the harbour. I may say that an adjustment has not yet been made with the owners of the property expropriated. The department is endeavouring to secure some basis upon which to make a settlement. Failing that the matter will be dealt with in the usual way through the exchequer court It is rather a unique case, of course, because I suppose the privately owned property could be said to be practically worthless unless and until the port works and railway are built. However, it will be for the exchequer court to determine what compensation should be paid. The pioneer settler who homesteaded there had faith that that was the proper port for the Hudson bay. While he is dead and gone, I do not think this parliament would like to see those who have succeeded him robbed of the results of his pioneer faith. However that may be, no doubt the exchequer court will pay due regard to all the considerations which should be taken into account. It is true that a substantial portion of the property has passed out of the hands of the original owner, Mr. Beech, and the Beech estate, and the ownership of lots is scattered in the subdivision. As to what will be done in the future, I know my hon. friend would like to see the government embark on an experiment of a town in which there was no private ownership.
Hear, hear.

I cannot say as yet if
it will be possible for us to work out anything of that sort in connection with the development at Churchill. The whole matter is under consideration. It is not the intention

of the government to dispose of any property to private individuals until the port development is thoroughly planned and we can see clearly what should be the next step in the development.

May I inquire of the
minister what arrangement, if any, has been made with the province of Ontario with regard to the right of way which was granted through Dominion lands to Port Nelson in 1913? If my memory serves me right, there was a strip of land five miles wide running from the boundary of Ontario to Port Nelson, the idea being that the province would have the opportunity of building the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway up to Port Nelson if she so desired. Does that arrangement carry to Churchill at the present time, or has any new arrangement been made with regard to it?

I am advised that the
old arrangement with regard to the right of way to Port Nelson lapsed some time ago. But however that may be, there would be no objection, indeed quite the contrary, to making such arrangements as might be necessary to enable the government of Ontario to extend their Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to Churchill if that government should so desire at any time. My information is that they are presently heading in the direction of James bay towards Moose Factory, rather than towards the west coast of the bay.

I understood we made a grant of the right of way. Were there any conditions attached to it that would cause it to lapse? I remember very well the discussion that took place here by reason of this territory being given to the province of Manitoba.

The condition was that
if they went on within a certain period the right existed. But in any case I can assure my hon. friend that we will have the whole matter looked into, and if it is necessary to extend any rights in that regard arrangements can easily be made. I am personally very doubtful of the desirability of giving one province a corridor five miles wide through another province. It would in my judgment be quite sufficient for the purpose of the province owning the railway if it were permitted to acquire a sufficient amount of land within the adjoining province to enable it to build its railway to the point it desired to reach. That has been done with respect to the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway entering the

Supply-Hudson Bay Railway
province of Quebec. It now enters that province, and although it has no corridor five miles wide it has of course the usual right to build a railway, which I am quite sure is satisfactory to the government of Ontario. In any case I assure my hon. friend that no difficulties will be placed in the way of the extension of the Ontario government railway to the port of Churchill if there is a desire that it should reach there.

It would be the province of Manitoba to whom we should have to go if Ontario so desired. I understand that this territory has now been made a part of the province of Manitoba. If we build a railway in Manitoba we shall have to go to that legislature.

My hon. friend forgets
that the land over which the line would pass is still in the crown in the right of this Dominion.
What right should we have to build a line in Manitoba?

By securing permission
from this government, just as the province of Ontario did in connection with the Temiskam-ing and Northern Ontario railway when it was desired to go into the province of Quebec. There was legal action in the matter, afterwards settled; and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway did secure the right to enter upon crown lands in the province of Quebec-crown lands which in that case were in the right of the province.
What is contemplated in the way of port expenditure at Churchill? Can the minister give us an estimate of what expenditure will be necessary to render the port satisfactory?

In engaging Mr. Palmer to make an investigation we asked him, in the letter of engagement, to give estimates based on a minimum port development. Perhaps I had better read the terms of the letter. This was what Mr. Palmer was asked to do, and it is the basis of the figures I am about to present:
What we have in mind as an initial test development and this is suggested more for your guidance than as a conclusive and limiting instruction-would be the provision of accommodation in either harbour for six cargo ships in port at one time, with working berths for three of the six; the estimated draught of the vessels to be not less than twenty-six feet. The minimum development projected at each port should, of course, be capable of such progressive extension as future requirements might dictate.
On that basis the harbour works at Churchill are estimated by Mr. Palmer to cost $8,450,159.
Including elevators?

That includes provision for an elevator having a capacity of a million bushels. In that connection I might say, particularly for the benefit of members from the west who are interested in the handling of grain, that my idea was that to start with, in an initial test development, it would be better to plan for a fast handling low capacity elevator which could subsequently be added to by means of additional storage as the route developed. But to start with, my calculations and those of the department indicated that a million bushel storage plant, with very fast handling capacity-the fastest which is at present in use-would be the most economical and satisfactory equipment.

Has the minister ever made any estimate of the total cost of the Hudson Bay development, embracing: the railway, port development, the money ahead}' expended there, the cost of bridges, aids to navigation and development in the straits? In other words, what is the estimated total cost of everything in connection with that development until it reaches, say, the eastern or the southern end of the strait, that is, the entrance to the strait from the Atlantic?

In that regard I can give information only as it affects the Department of Railways and Canals. The work on the straits is being conducted, as my hon. friend knows, by the Department of Marine. I have before me information relating to the Department of Railways. To date, since the inception of the Hudson Bay undertaking in 1911, there has been expended on the railway and port combined-everything-the sum of $28,333,711.72. That is up to March 31 last. As to the cost of completion, that is of course a matter of not so great certainty; but to complete the railway it is estimated that $7,543,000 will be required, and to complete the port $8,450,000. Roughly, therefore, the estimates would indicate fhat about $16,000,000 more will be required to complete the whole project, over and above what has been expended up to March 31 last.

Will it be in order for me to ask that the minister obtain from the Public Works department the cost of their expenditure?
Supply-Hudson Bay Railway

It would be the Department of Marine and Fisheries, whose minister is not here. I can tell my hon. friend, however, as regards expenditures by any other department, that they commenced only last year. The vote in the estimates last year and, I believe, also in the supplementaries, for the Department of Marine and Fisheries in connection with work on the straits represents the total expenditure up to date under that department. One great cuuse of all western Canada, as the minister himself knows, has been the appalling and unjustifiable speculation especially in city property of almost every kind. If the minister can prevent that in Churchill he will have performed a great service not only to his own department, but to the development of the port itself. If the rapid development of that port is to be forecast now and is to progress in the future, it will depend upon the absence of too heavy capitalization in land. If we can turn that money into the proper channels of development work and so on it will help to a very large degree, but when answering the hon. member for Wetaskiwin the minister stated that he was not certain that he could carry out the implied plans.
No, my hon. friend did not understand me correctly.

I am tryrMr. W. A. Black.]
ing to encourage the minister, and I would like him to go a little further in this matter.
I think he has announced a departure from the old, orthodox method which will mean a great deal to western Canada in the development of that north country, and if only he can be strengthened in his present state of mind to the degree where he will develop plans for the development of Churchill along these lines he will be doing a great deal for western Canada. Now I hope he can give us a little further information with respect to what he had in mind in this matter.

I am sorry my hon. friend misunderstood me, and possibly he has misunderstood the press statement to which he has made reference. The difficulty with which we were faced when Churchill was selected was an immediate difficulty with respect to the evils of speculation. Private individuals did own property at Churchill. What I was referring to then and what I am referring to now is the trouble which arose in that regard immediately Churchill was selected. Immediately the announcement was made an official of the department was sent to the land titles office in Manitoba to file the necessary expropriations. My hon. friend will realize the importance of that if for a moment he will imagine what would have happened before now if that action had not been taken. That was the point I had in mind. As to what we should do for the future, thait I intended to leave for more mature reflection, having regard to experience elsewhere in regard to similar matters, but il did desire and the government desired to prevent the sort of thing which certainly would have happened before now if the privately owned property had not been expropriated in the first place.
As to the plans for the future, I will admit that since that time I have been studying various methods which have been applied elsewhere in the world with respect to experiments of the character indicated by my hon. friend. Frankly, there is nothing in existence that I can find whioh is quite as ideal as some of my hon. friends would desire in that regard. Particularly is the development of anything of that sort difficult when you bear in mind that the whole of the property for thousands of miles around is owned by the crown. If my hon. friend will also bear in mind the attitude of the public towards property owned by the crown, from his experience in the west he will know that it has proven virtually impossible to prevent people from squatting on crown property, where it exists in large areas such as is the case around Churchill. One of the great problems in

evolving any plan for the development of Churchill along such lines as my hon. friend has in mind is that wherever crown property has existed in this country in large area, in practice it has been found impossible to prevent people from simply going in, sitting down and taking possession without acquiring any real rights and certainly no speculative rights, hindering development such as my hon. friend has in mind.

I think in

In any case, the squatter does not possess title to the land, nor can he acquire title except through the crown.
I mentioned that.

So even if the whole territory were surrounded by squatters the title is in the crown, and the crown can determine upon what terms the land may be further used by these persons. At the present time I am not going to enter into a discussion of a practical method by which this scheme can ibe applied; it is too late in the session for that, but I am going to meet the minister in this way: I am going to send him in writing a plan which has been worked out before and which may be applicable to the Churchill situation. I hope he will take it into
consideration; I feel sure he will, because on the whole I think he is rather inclined towards a little experiment in this matter, and if the suggestion is at all practical I think he will accept it.

Mr. Palmer was a very

The department is arranging, in fact it has had under way all winter a careful observation at both points and in addition we are intending to secure aeroplanes for an aeroplane observation of the ice conditions off both ports during the present summer and particularly during the period in the fall when both ports would necessarily be most interesting from that point of view. We are finding aeroplane transportation a very useful adjunct to our work in the north country and indeed mining people and others are using aeroplanes up there now. Having them, we intend to conduct a very thorough, careful and continuous comparison in regard to ice conditions at both ports. We have learned now what appears to be a regular condition and that is that the two ports are not at all comparable as to ice conditions. When the ice goes out at Churchill, it is gone. When the ice goes

out at the port of Nelson, it may not be, and very frequently is not clear of the mouth of the Nelson river, twenty odd miles away. It appears to be characteristic that the ice coming down from the north with the currents masks the entrance to the Nelson river long after the port of Nelson itself is free from ice. To simplify the explanation I might say to my hon. friend that it is very frequently possible to get by ship from Nelson twenty miles down stream while Churchill is frozen up, but it would be impossible to get from Nelson out to sea. Have I made that clear? That is one thing we have learned so far which appears to be very interesting and we are continuing the observations.

I can understand that, but what I am inquiring about is this. For instance I find under the contract with Johnson P. Porter, sections 1 and 2. the sheet piling is put down at six cents. I find in another contract by different people the price for the same item is five cents, making a difference of about $64,000 in the case of that one item. I am at a loss to understand how on the same job in returns made for the same year there should be so large a discrepancy.

The explanation of that is this: When the tenders were originally called for on each of these sections, contractors were asked to bid on the basis of unit prices for every operation involved. While the unit price might be lower the price in the aggregate might be higher. The man who bid a cent less, let us say, for sheet piling might be two cents more than another tenderer on material involving a far larger expenditure, and in letting the contract-most of them, of course, were made before my time, but some have been let since, and I have had the experience-I have always asked the accountants to extend the totals of the whole tender on unit prices aggregating everything 'n the tender.
On estimated quantities, of course?

Yes, and then awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer in the aggregate, based on unit prices. We have had the experience many times of one tenderer bidding a very low price on some very small item, but in the aggregate submitting a high tender as compared with the other tenderers.

this with another private car? Recently I was in a car which was not very sumptuously furnished, and I was told it cost $100,000. By comparison the cost of these cars does not look excessive.

My hon. friend will
appreciate how impossible it is to give comparisons with other private or business cars, for the reason that such cars vary in price anywhere up the scale as high as $200,000.

These are not the most
expensive cars.

Not by any means.
There are cars much more expensive on the road to this country, particularly the cars from the United States. Any railwayman will tell you that.

Will the minister answer this question? As this is a state affair, why should not the expenditure be shouldered by the state? Why should the Canadian National Railways be burdened with it, and the amount hidden so that no one can tell what it really is?

Answering my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary), the nearest comparison I have under my hand is for the New York Central. Last year that railroad furnished to its president and, I think, four vice-presidents, cars for their use at a cost of $100,000 each. I presume they would not be equipped in an unduly sumptuous manner for those officers. With reference to my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) it is just a matter of arrangement. Now that we have a state railway, I believe all our railway equipment should be owned by the railway. The railway can better look after it. If there is a maintenance account then let the government meet it with respect to any cars in the service. But as a matter of good business I think railway equipment owned by the government had better be owned by that agency of the government which has to do with railways, namely, the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:

Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, maintenance and operation, $287,100.

Item agreed to.
Welland ship canal

to provide for payment to P. Lyall and Sons Construction Company, Limited, on account of washing rock from section 4-not anticipated at time tenders were called for, $56,658.
Mr, GUTHRIE: Will the minister explain what this vote is? It is unusual, and I do not understand it.

This is the third time an item of this kind has appeared in the estimates with reference to the Welland canal. Following a great deal of difficulty from an engineering point of view on the question of washing rock, some three years ago it was finally decided that this work should be done, a schedule of payment with respect to it was arranged and agreed upon and of course in each of the succeeding years it had to be paid as an extra amount. I am informed that this is the last year during which this rock washing will be necessary; this will

Supply-Railways-Railway Commission
complete the work. This represents a grand total of 343.800 cubic yards, or 30,700 cubic yards less than the original estimate, and the total cost is $21,490 less than the original estimate.
May I ask the minister if the contract with the P. Lyall Company has been completed?
No.
What arrangement was made with that company by which they were allowed to sell part of their plant?

Back in 1919, just after the war, it was decided to proceed on the Welland canal by contract instead of having the government do the work, and in letting the various contracts each contractor had to take over part of the equipment then belonging to the government as part of his contract obligation. They are all paying for the equipment then purchased out of the amounts due on progress estimates from time to time, and the Lyall firm is in the same position.
When is it expected the Welland canal will be completed, and what is the total estimated cost?
I answered that this morning. It is expected to be completed by 1930 and will cost something between $115,000,000 and $120,000,000.
In just what position is the Lyall company in respect of its debt to the government?
Originally on the Lyall contracts $2,338,000 worth of machinery was purchased from the government, and there is a balance outstanding of $527,000 on that account.
How much machinery have they sold to others?
They are not allowed to sell any machinery until it is paid for. I may tell my friend that the account is being well protected by the engineers in charge.

I would like a little information with regard to this amount for washing rock. I think it was generally understood that the rock to be used in the concrete was to be excavated from the cuttings of the.canal. Who first brought up the question of this rook being washed before it was used in the concrete?

As I indicated before my hon. friend came in, this is the third occasion on which it has been necessary to introduce an item for this purpose. The basis was settled some three years ago, but probably my hon. friend does not recall the previous discussions. The original negotiations took place in 1925. It was part of the contract that this contractor should deliver to another contractor rock which was being excavated from his part of the canal. When the actual excavation of the rock was going on it was found that there was too much of an intermixture of clay; the rock was full of fissures of clay. Someone had to wash the rock and there was no provision in the contract for it; the contractor was merely obligated to deliver the rock, so these arrangements had to be made.
In other words this was (done to meet a condition which was not anticipated when the contract was let?
That is so.
What is the rate per cubic yard for washing this rock?
The rate is seventy cents per cubic yard; that is the actual cost, checked by our own officials.
How do you arrive at the rate of seventy cents as the actual cost?

We check the actual
operation.
How is it washed?
With big jets of water under pressure.

I should think seven cents would be more nearly correct than seventy cents for washing rock with jets of water. I do not care what the pressure is; the higher the pressure the more effective it would be. It seems to me that seventy cents is an outrageous price. What is the cost for excavating?
I can only say to my hon. friend that our officers and auditors check the actual cost of this operation.
I must take objection to that price, because never, by any possibility, could this operation cost as much as seventy cents per cubic yard.
What does it cost per cubic yard to excavate?

One class of material
costs $1.56, another class 60 cents, and another class $30 per yard. I am informed by

the officers of the department that these rates are affected by the distance and conditions regarding the disposal of the material after it is excavated, and they are hardly a criterion of the cost.
I cannot understand that material which can be excavated for 60 cents per yard should cost 70 cents per yard to wash.
It is earth that costs 60 cents.
I asked for the cost on rock.
That cost is $1.56.

Seventy cents is about
one-half, and there would appear to be something wrong there.
I will be glad to make inquiries. My officers inform me that an actual check has been kept ever since these operations started in 1926.
You had better put in a new set of officers.

Canadian government railways-to provide an additional car ferry between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, $1,000,000.
I wish to thank the minister for coming down off his perch and providing this vessel. I have now an answer to the question I asked in the committee on railways and shipping.

Item agreed to.
To supplement pension allowances payable under the provisions of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees' Provident Fund Act so as to make the minimum payment, during the period from January 1, 1928, to March 31, 1929, the sum of $30 per month instead of $20 as fixed by the said act, $50,000.
Will the employees get more this year than they did last year?

This vote has been necessary for a number of years in order to supplement the amounts paid in by the employees to the provident fund of the old Intercolonial railway. Due to a change in conditions throughout the years, this fund has run behind and it has been necessary for parliament to supplement it in order to enable the provisions of the provident fund to be carried out.
Is it the intention of the government to increase this amount next year?
The real reason for this deficit in the fund was that five or six years ago the minimum compensation was raised from $20 to $30, due to changed conditions, and this amount has been required.

I wonder if the Department of Railways and Canals or the minister have anything to do with the pensions of the Canadian National Railways' employees under the Provident Fund Act. There are some sad cases of employees who have been working for the railway for a number of years, such as that of Mr. Pierre Bosse of Riviere du Loup. Mr. Bosse has been working for the railroad for several years, and is entitled to a pension. He has paid his dues every year but the doctors refuse to give him a certificate that he is ill. I believe their reasons are that he has no wound in the face, and has the use of both eyes, and that he can hear; they believe he is all right. There are some doctors at the head office of the Atlantic region at Moncton who, I imagine, have not even yet received their diplomas; because they do not know how to examine sick people, and when employees go there the doctors stay on their throne and allow them to be looked after by their assistants who are just freshmen and know nothing about the diseases of the human body. I do not know if they could qualify even as veterinary surgeons. People who have given their lives to the Canadian National Railways, and who have paid annually to get a pension when they are sick or too old, have had trouble in getting what they are entitled to. I have personal knowledge of a man who was employed on the section at Trois-Pistoles who went down to Moncton to be examined. The doctor told him that he was perfectly well, but when he went to another doctor and was X-rayed it was found that he suffered from a very serious disease. When he brought back the plates to Moncton the Canadian National specialists had to acknowledge their mistake. I wish to bring the case of Mr. Pierre Bosse to the attention of the minister

Supply-Railways-Railway Commission
and of the house, because when the department ask for a vote of $50,000 to help the employees they should right any injustice that has been done. Mr. Bosse has worked for the railway almost twenty years, being laid off on account of staff reduction. He claimed his right of seniority, but that was not given to him. He wanted to work in the same capacity as he had worked before, but while he is a carpenter, they told him that he should fire a boiler. He was fifty-nine or sixty years old then and this was a very hard job for him. He could not do it because he was ill. When he reported his case again, they told him that it was a fake; that he was not serious. I think the way in which old employees are treated by the officials of the company in the Canadian National medical branch at Moncton is a shame. The matter should be brought to the attention of the house and I hope the minister, although there is a wall between him and the Canadian National railway management, will be able to make an opening through the wall large enough to enable him to tell them to be fair to their employees and to give them what is due to them.

Item agreed to.
Pensions-J. L. Weller, $3,500.

What are
these for?

This is just one item. I
have under my hand all the information regarding every one of these votes. If it is not given, it is simply because no one appears to desire it. In most cases the explanation has been given in previous years and I do not like to inflict the explanations on the committee unless they are asked. Mr. Weller was employed by the government for forty-two years as an engineer. He was never in the position of being a permanent civil servant. He entered the service of the department in 1883 as an engineer on canal construction and operation. In 1900 he was appointed superintending engineer of the Welland canal, which office he held until 1912 when he was appointed engineer in charge of survey and design of construction of the then proposed new Welland ship canal. He remained in charge of the work until 1917 when it was closed down owing to the war, and Mr. Weller's services were dispensed with. From January, 1919, to March 31, 1927, the services of Mr. Weller were retained in the capacity of consulting engineer in connection with the construction of the Welland ship canal, and his salary was fixed at $3,600 per annum, it being felt that that rate was adequate in view of the fact that his whole time was not being
occupied during that period. Mr. Weller is now well on in the seventies and in view of his record of service, which, had he been in the permanent class of civil servants, would have undoubtedly entitled him to superannuation, a year ago the house voted this pension for him. It is on the basis of the Calder Act.

This is
Bimply putting Mr. Weller in the same class as retired judges.

No, putting him in the
position that he would have been in as a permanent civil servant retiring under what are known as the provisions of the Calder Act.
He did not pay anything into the superannuation fund?
No.
In that sense he is receiving superannuation the same as retired judges, who never pay anything into the superannuation fund.

speakeroldname: Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: The increase in this appropriation is due mainly to a revision of salaries, slight increases in living allowances for trade commssioners and an increase to provide for an increase in the number of commissioners on account of the growth in the service. Item agreed to.
Dominion Bureau of Statistics, $150,000.

Why the reduction? It
is so rare that we would like an explanation.

The Bureau of Statistics, as my hon. friend will recollect, always has a larger staff when the quinquennial census is on and in a near census period. The bureau happens to be decreasing its staff now. The quinquennial census in Saskatchewan is over and I think there will be a smaller staff for the next year or two until the next census.

My reason for asking was because the Bureau of Statistics is one of the departments of the government for which I have a great deal of respect. You can get quick and reliable information in a very short time. I like to say a good word once in a while for some branches of the service because I think we are a little inclined to be over critical. That is why I particularly noticed the reduction.

I wish also to associate myself with the remarks of my hon. friend from Fort William. I think there are few departments which have been

pursuing so constantly useful a service to the members of this house as the Bureau of Statistics. I regret to see a reduction because, although the minister speaks of the quinquennial census as having passed by, yet I do know as a result of questions. I have asked Doctor Coats that there is much material still to be gathered, much synchronizing of the work of various collecting agencies, much tabulating and inter-relating of facts with respect to various works and developments throughout the country still to be done. I would suggest to the minister, whom I look upon as one of the most intelligent members of the ministry, and that is paying quite a compliment to the rest of the ministers, that when we come to agricultural statistics in particular, the Department of Trade and Commerce unfortunately is sadly lacking in the required personnel. I have found that through personal investigation, and I am perfectly satisfied that Doctor Coats could do with several assistants in that particular branch of his work.
There is another question which comes up at this stage. I wonder whether it would not be possible for the minister to consider the possibility of amalgamating two or three of the other statistical branches of this department with the Bureau of Statistics. That would result in greater uniformity, and in the elimination of some overhead and some overlapping that is existing at the present time, and on the whole I think the minister would find that it would result in more satisfactory work.
My principal objection to this reduction- it is very seldom that I object to a reduction -is that I am satisfied as a result of my own investigation that the Bureau of Statistics could do with additional personnel, particularly in the agricultural staff. For example, I go down there and ask for information respecting the capitalization of manufacturing industry in Canada. I get that information, and I go further and say that I would like to have a return showing the average wage paid and the total wages paid in manufacturing industries, and that I want the same information with regard to agriculture. But in agriculture I can only get an estimate, and that is very vague. I go still further. When I want to tabulate the relative economic value of agriculture to manufacturing, with absolute facts and figures, I am always given the answer:	We can give you this information
with respect to manufacturing fairly accurately, but not with respect to agriculture. I think in a country of this size, and in view

Supply-Trade and Commerce
of the paramount importance of agriculture, the minister will find that his department will not lose, and the country will not lose, by giving Doctor Coats all possible help in that direction. I compliment the minister, and particularly Doctor Coats, on the very excellent work which has been done in the past.

Can the minister say
when the bureau will be moved out of that firetrap in which it is now located? The Minister of Public Works told us some five weeks ago that the bureau would be moved out in six weeks, but from the look of the building at New Edinburgh I would say that it would be six weeks longer. In the event of a fire occurring in that building, with such crowded quarters, there would not only be the loss of valuable statistics, but the much more important loss of human life very probably, and I would just like to give this warning to the minister.

I think everyone appreciates the danger of the quarters which the bureau is now in, and just as rapidly as the property which . we are taking over, which fortunately is fireproof, can be got ready, the bureau will be moved.
Mr. Cf)OTE: When the Minister of Public
orks slated that the Bureau of Statistics was going to be moved to the old mill at New Edinburgh, I thought it was the wrong place to put the bureau. It is too far away from the parliament buildings and from other government departments, with which the bureau must be in constant communication for the gathering of statistical information. I think the government might even yet consider placing the bureau in some building adjacent to the other departments of government, and certainly closer to the parliament buildings. I think it is an awful mistake to place the bureau away out there at New Edinburgh.

amount of electric energy exported?

I have the details if
my hon. friend would like me to read them. The licenses cover a total- export of electric energy amounting to 291,525 kilowatts. Fees paid amount to $675, and the export duties collected to $267,652.

From what province is that
exported?

I think from almost
every province in Canada. It is exported by the Hydro Electric Commission of Toronto, Canadian Niagara Power Company, West Kootenay Power Company, Southern Canada Power Company, International Electric Power Company, Maritime Electric Power Company, and the Fraser-Power Company, of Edmundston, New Brunswick, and others.
Not the Hydro Electric Commission, of Toronto: it is the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission.

The Ontario Hydro

Item agreed to.
National Research Council, $300,000.
Does the research work carried on at Winnipeg into the rust problem come under this vote?
Yes.

There is a big increase in this vote; can the minister explain it?



Supply-Trade and Commerce

We had a discussion of this item before, but I shall be glad to read from the brief again:
This vote is required to provide for the general activities of the National Research Council, including the organization, co-ordination and stimulation of research -work in Canada; grants in aid of scientific and industrial researches; special problems; scholarships for the post-graduate training in science and research of the best scientific talent graduating from Canadian universities, for service in the industries of Canada and in the technical departments of the government service; salaries of staff; general administration, and for such other purposes as the council may deem necessary in order to effectively carry on and extend its activities.
The sum of $170,000 was voted by parliament for the work of the council during the fiscal year 1927-28. The vote requested this year therefore represents an increase of $130,000 over the vote for 1927-28. _
This increased vote is required in order to effectively carry on the activities of the voluntary research organization, which has been built up by the council during the last ten years and which is steadily expanding along sound lines.	.
The National Research Council is charged with the functions and duties detailed in sections six and ten of the Research Council Act.
The act provides for a council of fifteen members, each of whom, with the exception of the president, serves in an honorary capacity, without remuneration, for a period of three years, one-third of the membership retiring each year. Under the act, the council is constituted a corporate body, capable of accepting and holding gifts, grants, bequests, etc., for the purpose of its work. All receipts and expenditures of the council are subject to examination by the Auditor General.
The president of the council may be a permanent officer, giving his full time to the work of the council.
The president of the council has given up his position as president of the Edmonton university and will now be in definite charge of the work.
Has the minister dropped the somewhat elaborate program that he outlined earlier this session?

Not at all. That was to provide for the permanent laboratories of the council; this is the administration vote. This $130,000 increase is necessary this year to carry on the work of the council while the new quarters are being provided.
When do you expect that to take place?
I did not catch my hon. friend's question.
How much money is spent on research work in Ottawa?

I cannot give my hon. friend an answer. I believe there are three

separate research investigations going on: one by the National Research Council, another by the Board of Grain Commissioners, and a third by the Department of Agriculture.
Have the National Research Council their own investigators that are being paid out of the moneys voted under this item?
Yes, everything is paid out of this item with respect to their own investigations.
I think the rust research work is carried on partly by the Department of Agriculture.

The Department of
Agriculture is conducting research work on the rust problem independently of the work that is being done by the Board of Grain Commissioners in their laboratories at Winnipeg. The National Research Council is making a contribution to that work.

I understand that the building which is being used for rust research work at Winnipeg was built out of moneys voted to the Department of Agriculture, and the work is being done by its officials. Am I correct?

If my hon. friftid is referring to the work that is being done by the Manitoba College, the money was voted by the Department of Agriculture, but the research work that is being carried on by the Board of Grain Commissioners in connection with the rust problem comes under the Trade and Commerce department vote.

In connection with the resignation of one or two of the officials who were engaged in the rust research work at Winnipeg, were they in the employ of the National Research Council or of the Department of Agriculture?
They must have been in the employ of the Department of Agriculture, because we have had no men leave our staff.
Will the classification and salaries of the men who are in the employ of th National Research Council come under the Civil Service Commission?

I think my hon. friend understands that a great many of the technical men engaged in rust research work are not employees of the government at all'; they are professors of the universities in the west. We make contributions to their salaries Only part of their time is devoted to rust research work, and they do not come under the Civil Service Commission.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I want to ascertain whether the National Research Council engages these men. One of the men I had in mind is Mr. Bailey. I believe he has left the service either of the Department of Agriculture or of the National Research Council.
The Department of Agriculture.

The rust research work is extremely important to western Canada. As I understand, only a few thousand dollars per annum are spent on this work, whereas the loss to the grain crop of western Canada during the past few years has been tremendous. It would be well for whatever department is handling this work to consider very seriously the extension of its operations. In some seasons we have lost as much as 8150,000,000 from rust. As against this appalling loss we are spending only about $50,000 in trying to cope with the rust problem. I think this is one place where the government might spend a large sum of money until we find some commercial preventive for rust, and I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce, along with the ministers of any other departments concerned, would take seriously into consideration the expenditure of more money on this very important research work.

Mr. Chairman, last Saturday a gentleman greatly interested in research work drew my attention to the overlapping in this connection. The Fisheries department and the Agriculture department are carrying on research work, and the Interior department has almost a research branch of its own. Now you have the Department of Trade and Commerce. Cannot we do something to save the country's money by co-ordinating the efforts of these various departments? You will not get these various departments to relinquish their activities unless you strangle them by withholding money for the purpose. The officials of the Interior department will insist on carrying on their little show in connection with coal, iron and other things, the fisheries department will insist on their experts dealing with their problems, and the Agriculture department will never let go their particular work. At the present moment there is a waste of money. It has been found in the United States, Great Britain and Germany that the only way to do research work effectively is to bring it under one control, and until that is dune neither Doctor Tory nor anyone else will make a success of it. If he
56103-237*
is made chairman of the research council he must have control of all the research work carried on in this country by the various branches of government departments.

speechtext: Not only do Doctor Grisdale and Doctor Camsell sit on the research council, but they are parties to the program of research work prepared by the council. So far we have not had laboratories under the control of the research council. My hon. friend knows that full well.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I will deal
with the Interior department in a minute. For the present I am dealing with the two departments my hon. friend has been criticizing. So far there have been no laboratories other than those provided by the departments of Agriculture and Mines to carry on this work, and only such work as should be carried on has been undertaken by these two departments. But that does not mean that they cannot be co-ordinated with the research council. Not for a single moment does it mean that. They have been coordinated, and I wish to assure my hon. friend that there has been no overlapping in any work that has been done. I cannot speak so authoritatively in respect of fisheries; there may have been in the Fisheries department. But I can speak for the work done in the Mines department as well as in Agriculture

Supply-Trade and Commerce
because both these gentlemen are fully conversant with the program set out by the research council. That is why I rise to put my hon. friend right on the question. As I say,
I cannot-speak with equal authority in regard to fisheries, but 1 shall be glad to know the point at which there has been duplication of work as between the research council and the fisheries department. I should also be glad to know, if my hon. friend would tell me, where there is interference, on. the part of the research work carried on in the wood products laboratory in the Department of Interior, with the research council's program, because I have tried to avoid such overlapping. I do not say that co-ordination should not take place; I am all for it and will use every effort to ensure coordination, so far as I am able to bring it about. I repeat, however, that so far there has been no overlapping as suggested. To say that there has been overlapping in all departments is not borne out by the facts.

I am sdrry the minister
has not accurately followed my observations. Several departments are independently expending public moneys. That is the point I was endeavouring to make. These departments are independently spending the money in research work, and that should not be. Whoever is responsible for research work should spend the money. The Department of the Interior, as we know, and as was pointed out the other evening, has buildings and is spending public moneys in research work. The Department of Agriculture is also being voted money for research work; the fisheries department is voted money for research work; and the mines branch is also being voted money for the same purpose. The point I wish to make is that if the organi-ation -which is now taking over research work i3 to succeed it must have control over these operations. It is idle to say that some gentleman associated with the Department of the Interior or some deputy minister of mines are members of this research council, for as indicated by the minister the other evening-it is not necessary to repeat it-the research council has certain duties to perform. This is clear: so long as parliament makes votes to various departments who may independently spend these moneys, as they are now doing, co-ordination, and overlapping are not only inevitable but follow from day to day. The minister speaks of wood products; there is about as much necessity for that work as carried on as there is for a fifth wheel to a coach. The University of McGill was endeavouring to carry on that work, but

the Department of the Interior wanted it and got it. And we are voting public money for it. If you are to have one department to carry on this work, let all moneys be voted to that department; but do not make separate grants to separate departments for research activities. That is my point and that is the point to which I direct the attention of the minister. The fact that Doctor Grisdale or Doctor Camsell is a member of the council is beside the point; the point is that this country is asked to grant sums of money to be expended independently by various departments of the public service, whereas the whole matter should be in the hands of the research department.
