I wish to emphasize the observation that there is want of co-ordination and waste of money at the present time. I would direct the attention of the committee to the statement of the president of the council as to the duties of that body. I am strongly in sympathy with the work and I am a strong supporter of research, but I must condemn the results we are obtaining at present. The duties of the council, as indicated by the president, are these: first, to promote the utilization of the natural resources of Canada; second, to undertake researches with the object of improving technical processes and methods used in the industries of Canada, and of discovering processes and methods which may promote the expansion of existing or the development of new industries; and, third, to undertake researches with a view to the utilization of the waste products of industry. I shall discuss only two or three things to show that there is a waste of money as well as a want of co-ordination in the work, judging from the results. Take fishing, for example. There is a biological board going into research work in the fisheries. That board has published a report on the oyster, a report which this government has never attempted to implement. There is also the report of a commission requesting the enforcement of the recommendations of the
biological 'board. So much for that; it will stand a good deal of study. In the next place we have the work done in the mines branch. I would ask the committee this question: What is the use of publishing all these books on chemical and metallurgical development, on arsenic, the survey of Canada for arsenic, fuel ore, testing and so forth? Here are reports from the research committee which the government has ignored in its budget. What is ore testing except examining the tailings of mining plants and of smelters? They are trying to find some way of making use of these things, yet with that in mind this government have admitted into Canada the materials which go into the manufacture of insect poisons and insecticides. Here was an opportunity to use our low grade ores throughout the country; the Department of Mines published a big book on arsenic, containing a survey of the arsenical ores of Canada, and yet we import from the United States all these articles, among them arsenic in large quantities.
This is a subject on which I could speak for a long time, but I am going to stop now. The report of the Department of Mines draws attention to the fact that the time has now arrived when low grade ores should be considered and used, yet by our budget wc have taken away an opportunity to make use of them. I have here a list of thirty-three industries in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia using these low grade ores of which arsenic is one of the most important byproducts. For years arsenic was a white elephant at all smelters; no- use could be found for it, but finally the discovery was made that it was a very good insecticide. The United States supply was used up in two years, but they surveyed their fields and at present they have all their arsenical ores located. We have just completed our survey, yet now that we have an opportunity to build up new industries which will give employment to our people, by our budget we have wiped o-ut any possibility of using these ores. For that reason I say there is a great lack of co-operation >in this work which is being carried on. I approve of the work done by the research council, but I do condemn the government for the use they have made of the reports and recommendations made by that body.

I am sorry this vote is so small. I should like to know how much money has been spent on rust research, but

Supply-Trade and Commerce
since part of this work is under the Department of Trade and Commerce and part under the Department of Agriculture it seems impossible to secure that information. However, -if the total amount of this vote were spent on rust research it would be much too small. One of the three professors at the agricultural college at Winnipeg, has made a discovery in connection with rust which has s(t|artled the sctientifiq men of the North American continent, yet we have lost this man and possibly two others simply because they were not being paid sufficient salaries. The hon. member for Moose Jaw stated that hi some years our loss from rust amounted to 8150,000,000, and I think he was not. far over the mark. I doubt if the loss would average that much year by year, but for the last four or five years a conservative estimate of the loss would be $50,000,000 per year, ana that is increasing annually. If this vote is any indication of the amount of money being spent on rust research, the sum is altogether too small, and I hope the minister will see that in another year this work is pushed on and a larger amount expended in that connection.
There is another question I should like to ask, although I do not know whether or not the minister will be able to give me the information. I wish to know whether the places of those men who have left the service have been filled. That does not come under this department, so perhaps I cannot expect it from the minister, but if he has that information I shall be glad to get it.

I think my hon. friend realizes that up to the present the National Research Council has contributed grants in aid of research to our laboratories. I am sorry the information before me is not definite in connection with the grants; they are not divided, although the total amount of money granted in aid of research last year is $170,000. How much of that was actually granted for rust research I cannot say, but I can assure my hon. -friend that with a larger vote this year that grant will be increased accordingly, and that when the laboratories of the research council in Ottawa are in operation, with the council directing the research work of Canada in general, as I hope will be the case in years to come, very sympathetic consideration will be given the question of rust research.

On the
question of the co-ordination of the activities of the various research branches, I do not

think even the leader of the opposition could point to any single country in which there is complete co-ordination; I do not think that is possible. I think in every country we will find that certain needs arise in certain industries and that certain universities will be carrying on certain lines of investigation. That is the situation in Canada, and as far as research in agriculture is concerned, I would hesitate quite a long while before recommending that the entire administration and direction of agricultural research should be placed completely under the control of the National Research Council. I am afraid that at times, in all countries, scientific men assume positions of directorship without hav-the agricultural viewpoint, and if you take away that important viewpoint from a scientific body such as the National Research Council, we might find ourselves in serious difficulties in the future. However, I do think that co-ordination can be sensibly and logically carried to the point where direction may be secured from some central body, while the actual research work itself might remain under the auspices of the particular department concerned.

I am not sure that this is
the proper place to bring to the attention of the government the importance of the rust epidemic in western Canada, but I presume it will be appropriate here. It has been my experience in talking to people of this section of the Dominion that they do not grasp the significance of this outbreak of rust in western Canada. Very often when I mention it they say, "The whole trouble is that you fellows do not go into mixed farming." I should like to spend a good deal of time on this subject, but I will simply make a few statements.
The first statement I want to make is regarding the growing of hard wheat in western Canada. This has put western Canada on the map; if that country had been left to the development of dairying and mixed farming a good portion of it would still be a 'wilderness. Not so many years ago you could go down into the central states as far as Wisconsin and you would find that a large portion of the crop consisted of wheat, while to-day there
is practically no wheat grown. That movement has been coming north, and to-day Manitoba is not producing twenty-five per cent of the hard wheat she should be producing. Her crop last year was less than half what we consider her average crop should be, and of that half less than fifty per cent was hard wheat and the rest durum.
This rust area has spread until it practically reaches the northern section of the wheatgrowing area of Manitoba. It is now extending west; it has covered a large area of Saskatchewan and has reached into Alberta. The only remaining area for the wheat grower to recede into is the Peace River country. This epidemic has continued for many years, and we have reached the point where we have to put our backs to the wall and fight, because there is no area in western Canada left for wheat. When western Canada has to stop growing wheat we shall have lost our best means of return. This is the position so far as the rust question is concerned, and I hope the government and the business men of this section of the country will realize the facte as they are and endeavour to face them. The small amount of money we are expending in an endeavour to find some means of overcoming this epidemic is pitiful. We have the development of wheats which are rust-resisting; some of our scientists are talking about parasites to overcome the difficulty, while others maintain that cultural methods may be successful. The field is so broad that $50,000 or less is not going to make very much of an impression on this very important matter. When it was being discussed the other day the Minister of Finance told us that the salaries of the scientific men were controlled by the Civil Service Commission. If the Civil Service Commission can obtain a man who is a graduate of some recognized college, who has taken post-graduate work, and has four years' experience in that special line, at a salary of $2,760, I will have no particular complaint to make just now. But it seems to me unreasonable to expect a man to come in and undertake investigation of such a broad field as the rust question at such a salary.
The amount we are spending on this problem seems to me to be like tossing a pebble in the ocean, so far as the effect is concerned. I am not going to enlarge on this in any way, but I do want to impress on the government and this country the significance of this question. Rust is driving the grain growing areas into the extreme north of the country, and large sections which are adapted to the grow-

mg of wheat in every way are practically put out of business on account of this scourge. I do hope that in the near future the government will spend a sufficiently large sum of money to be able to cope with this extremely serious situation.

In connection with the films that are sent out of the country, may I suggest that the pictures showing Canada should deal more largely with scenes showing fruit areas, farming areas, sport areas and our lakes and streams than they now do? I have heard it remarked often by people living outside of this country that we show too many winter scenes. People living in the southern states and elsewhere come to regard Canada as "Our Lady of the Snows" rather than as an agricultural country having a milder climate. We in Canada know the conditions that exist at different seasons of the year, but people living in the southern states, with whom I have come into contact, owing very largely to films showing winter scenes, have views regarding Canada which are rather astonishing. These pictures are very beautiful no doubt, but I would suggest that the department see to it that the films shown deal more with matters such as those I have mentioned.
I should like to ask the minister just exactly what these scenes cover? Do they take in the whole of Canada?

The best answer I can give to my hon. friend would be to ask him to pay a visit to the motion picture bureau and see some of the films. They cover a very broad range of industrial activities throughout the whole of the Dominion. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Pettit) asked that certain stress be laid on the class of film that would depict Canada as being a warmer country than it is depicted by some others. This is not a large vote; it is only a matter of $50,000 for the whole service, and we have to endeavour to secure all classes of films to represent all classes of industry, agriculture, fruit-growing, mining, pulp and paper, fishing. I think the director can hardly be criticized for being unfair to any one class of industry. He has divided up his films covering all industries and all parts of Canada as well as can reasonably be expected. Those who have seen the full range of films have never criticized the division. My hon. friend can get a catalogue of the films we have in the bureau. I shall be glad to send him one and to let him see the class of films that are shown.

An important point is that of attracting tourists. For instance, Cape Breton is one of the most beautiful spots in Canada and I have not seen any films pertaining to Cape Breton for the purpose of encouraging the tourist traffic. I think it would be a good idea to have views of the Bras d'Or lakes shown so that tourists may be attracted by their scenic beauty and fishing possibilities.

Has the
minister under consideration the appointment of any more trade commissioners in the United States?

That is rather a difficult question for me to answer. I doubt if any two men would agree on the number of trade commissioners we should have in United States. We would have asked for a larger appropriation for the commercial intelligence service this year had we the number of men in training and trained to send to the field, but at the present time we have not many men in training. My only
purpose in bringing the matter up was that in Canada in practically every city of importance we have a United States consular agent who does largely the work of one of our trade commissioners. He gathers all the business information that is required, and sends it back to the bureau that was established by Mr. Hoover, and the result is that you can

Supply-Trade and Commerce
go into the bureau at Washington and secure information about Canada and about business in any section of the country that you could not secure in many of our own cities, and it just occurred to me to suggest to the minister a way out of his difficulties. I am informed that the total fees paid for consular certificates and vises of all kinds for 1925 amounted to $1,137,000, and that the amount collected for invoice vises granted by the consular agents of the United States amounted to $459,346, while the total expenditure for the whole United States consular service in Canada was only $370,080; so there was a balance to the credit of the United States consular service of $1,226,000. If these figures be accurate- I have them only on hearsay-they do point the way out for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He could secure consular representation of this country in the United States, and have our agents do this investigational work and the gathering of information, just as the United States consular agents do here. For example, in the city of Calgary the United States consular agent appears every morning with the secretary of the board of trade, and inquires if there is anything to report to-day, any news at all. He also attends the meetings of the chamlber of commerce, and goes around and has a chat with the different members, and if there is anything new moving, any new development in connection with the tar sands or mineral deposits or any discoveries in oil, the information is passed on to the Hoover bureau in Washington. A service of the same magnitude may not be required by this country, but the functions of this department might well be broadened to include an active propaganda looking to the development of the home market to the same degree that you are working for the development of external markets. I have no doubt the minister has already this matter under advisement because he is not only intelligent, as I said, but he has a lot of vision. I think he might well take into consideration the possibility of establishing some sort of service such as I have suggested, which would not only be self-sustaining, but might in time return a handsome profit annually.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to

The minister is already aware that a large petition was signed by the people of Queen Charlotte islands for a better service, but their prayer was not granted because of the expenditure involved. It means that thousands of tourists who were anxious to take the Alaska trip will not be able to do so. I believe it is imperative that the

Canadian National put two new boats on the Alaskan trip, and that they should provide an improved service to Queen Charlotte islands, and also to Anyox, the smelter city, and to Stewart, which to-day is in the centre of the greatest mining development that British Columbia has known for many years. I should like the minister seriously to consider that proposition. Last year I wished to go down to Vancouver, but being a local resident it was impossible for me to book a passage on any of the tourist boats. A week ago I was in Montreal, and I found there the congestion was just as great as in Vancouver. When we consider that our tourist trade is the third greatest revenue producer surely every effort should be made to encourage it by improving our steamship and other services. I am told that two million tourists passed through Ontario last year. I contend that in our steamship service we are lagging far behind present-day requirements. I trust an effort will be made by the minister before another year to improve both the island service and the tourist service from Vancouver to Skagway.

When this vote was last before the committee we had two excellent addresses from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mae-phail). I am sure we all agree that peace is a good thing. In fact when I left Calgary I met no less a personage than Major General Archibald Macdonnell, who made a strong statement to me. He said, " Don't ever think that a general who has seen his men gassed, cut up and blown to pieces wants another war like the last I feel sure that all members of the house, whether they are returned soldiers or not, have a common desire for peace. The addresses of my hon. friends who spoke the other evening remind me very much of an incident related by Doctor Michael Clark, who once sat in this house. When in England during the Boer war he held a peace meeting in ithe town of Newcastle-on-Tyne. In the course of the meeting a number of soldiers and others in favour of the war broke in and disturbed the meeting by singing Soldiers of the Queen and other war songs. I said, "And doctor, what did you do in that case?" He said, A few of us old football players went at them and threw them out by the scruff of the neck ". I observed thait this was a rather belligerent method for a lover
Supply-National Defence

of peace to adopt, and he replied that he loved peace so well that he could fight for it. The speeches made by my two friends the other evening are what I should call fighting speeches for peace, while the speech made by the Minister of National Defence was a pacific speech for militia.
In all fairness .to the department and to the government itself it must be said that their record shows that they are not altogether war lords. During its term the government has expressed itself several (times in favour of any movement for peace. When I raised the question of the signing of the optional clause by Canada, one minute before six the Minister of Justice took occasion to declare that the government would support the optional clause. And while my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) was discussing the matter the other day the Prime Minister himself rose and stated that the Minister of Justice had spoken for the government and that they would gladly take any opportunity that offered to advance the cause of peace. Last Friday night the Prime Minister laid on the table the invitation of the United States to join in a multilateral peace treaty and the reply of Canada, which was favourable. So I think in all fairness to the government it might be termed a peace government, but with that, even though I do not .regard the Minister of National Defence as a war lord or the government as a war government, the minister must be prepared for a very searching inquiry as we go through these estimates. I rather think he will not resent it; he should not do so, and he dhould be able to give very good reasons why these estimates are being increased. I do not think I should say anything more at the moment, but as we go through these estimates, I shall take occasion, together with other hon. members, to subject the minister to some very close questioning.

Item agreed to.
Cadet services, $500,000.
I would like to ask the minister if the department are doing all they can to form additional cadet corps throughout Canada, and what methods are being followed?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Last year I described to the committee rather in detail just what is done under this vote. The system is that selected personnel are given special courses in physical training and cadet drill. Then they go to the Royal Military college, where further selections are made from those who have been

trained in the districts and further courses given. Then they are loaned to the various provincial governments and are sent to the normal schools, where they give those taking the normal course training in physical culture. That has been the system under which the physical training and cadet drill have been given. Then if there are those in the normal schools or in the districts who desire cadet training, a special course is established for them at district headquarters and they are given that training *which is necessary to equip teachers who desire to take up cadet work, and these teachers carry on that work in their various schools.

When we bring up any other thing pertaining to the field of education in this house we are always told that education is under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and that the Dominion Government must not interfere. How does the Minister of National Defence account for the fact that his is the only department which has anything to say about education in the different provinces?

I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension, or else she did not listen to my explanation last year. No cadet training is carried on without the consent of the provincial authorities; all we do is provide a fund for training teachers, if the provincial authorities desire such training.
Then in the opinion of the minister there would be nothing to prevent the Dominion government from teaching peace through the schools as aggressively as we now teach cadet training?

I repudiate the soft impeachment as to aggression; I am merely stating what we do. We provide this fund for the training of teachers who desire to take it, who take up that work in their schools where it is desired. There is nothing at all to prevent the establishment of some special chair for teaching peace, and it seems to me that what the federal government are doing right along, for instance in connection with those films which were referred to a few moments ago, is inculcating in the youth of our land a love of Canada and an appreciation of the activities of this country, which my hon. friend herself has mentioned. That is being done by the federal government. I have no doubt that if hon. members searched their minds they could remember other ways in which the federal authorities are indirectly assisting in connection with education in the schools.

Sup-ply-National Defence
But woulld you not call it aggression when the instructors are specially trained and specially paid by the government, and when uniforms, rifles and other equipment are supplied?

My hon. friend may come to any conclusion she wishes; I am simply stating what is done, leaving myself in the judgment of the committee and of the country as to whether or not it is aggressive. I say it is a perfectly proper and laudable thing for this government to provide such a fund for these provinces which desire this training to be carried on. No teacher is compelled to take up this work; no school is compelled to accept it. I can think of two schools in Manitoba, and there are many others, where the teachers who are directors of physical culture were trained by our instructors but where no cadet training is being carried on.

If the teachers in the various schools who give cadet training were not specially paid by the department and if their training were not provided out of the public funds, in the opinion of the minister would not that do something to lessen the demand of the provinces for cadet training?

I never was a teacher and I do not know what the attraction would be; I would leave that to my hon. friend to answer. I respectfully suggest that she should know whether or not a teacher would be attracted by what is paid in connection with this work, and I think I should leave it there.

I feel that I cannot let this vote go without saying something about it; reasons may be given why we should talk peace while we are increasing our military estimates and with those reasons the house may agree, but in connection with this vote I do not think any reasonable person can agree with the reasons given. Each year I have made a speech on this question and I am sure the house is very tired of hearing me talk about it. However, it seems to me that my opinions have been very well expressed by Rennie Smith, a member of the British house, so to begin with I will just put it in his words:
We have a right to safeguard our public education from the blight of a military state. We have a duty to protect our educational institutions from the encroachments of a zealous war office.
I believe that word "zealous" would also apply to this department.
It is in the schools, in the shaping of young minds, that the foundations of wars are laid.
I do not think that is putting it too strongly, and I do believe that the teaching of youngsters that the way to settle international disputes is to resort to war absolutely prevents them from thinking of any other way out. It seems to me a contradiction in terms and a hypocritical position for this or any other government to give lip service to peace while aggressively pushing the military machine into the schools of the country. The two things do not agree at all.
I had a very interesting debate with Major General MacBrien, former chief of the general staff, in Montreal; he was upholding cadet training in schools, and he took the ground that it was good physical training, that it was good discipline, that it brought security and that it is human nature to fight. Those were the grounds on which he debated, and wherever you hear this question discussed those points are brought up. I do not think any one of the four contentions is sound, and I am going to take just a little time to go rapidly through the same notes which I used on that occasion, but at much less length.
I would like to say that I had a most enjoyable time, and I wish we could have this discussion repeated about a dozen times throughout Canada. The purpose of education is to draw out the latent powers of the child or the adult who is being educated; to develop the initiative of that person, to develop his full rounded powers and to help him to fit himself to the community in which he lives and to render the best possible service. It seems to me that cadet training does not meet that definition of education. Military training subordinates the will of the individual and kills initiative, rather than developing it. I think that is very well expressed in the poem:
Tbeir's not to reason why,
Their's blit to do and die:
And let us hope there will not be any more die. In military training the individual cannot select what he is to do, and do it in the way he thinks best. If he is to become efficient he must become machine-like, and the result is that instead of raising a generation of youth who will shape society by their thoughts, they are shaped to the thought of existing society, which is very bad for both the child and society.
Is my hon. friend quoting?

No, but I will now quote from John Stuart Mill, who says that all attempts by the state to bias the conclusions of its subjects on disputed points are evil.

Supply-National Defence
There is no doubt at all that the Department of National Defence is trying to bias the opinion of people on a disputed point through cadet training. In Canada we are divided into two schools of thought on how to gain security, but the department is not .putting forward the two ways of getting security; they are only putting forward one. They are putting forward military training, military preparedness, the establishment of a military machine which can be turned against our enemies. They are trying to bias the minds of growing children on a disputed point, and a very important point too.
We now come to the question of physical training. It is very true that everyone needs physical training; whether boy or girl, youth or adult, physical training is needed to keep us fit. Military training alone is not good physical training, but in the past a great deal of what is purely physical training has been taken over by the military. During the war physical training occupied a great deal of the soldier's time, it being needed in order to keep him fit. I do not think military training appeals to the cadets; if we could give them the choice I believe they would take straight physical exercises, track work or work in the gymnasium; they would prefer that to military training. My conversations with many people would lead me to believe that to be true.
About a year and a half ago a survey was made in British Columbia by two educational experts, Dr. Putman of Ottawa and Dr. Weir of the university of British Columbia. They made an investigation, not only on this aspect of it but on many others, and in their report they said this:
We take strong exception to the plan of having any part of this work done by militia officers, who naturally give it a military bent.
And they say again:
We think the schools -would suffer no real loss if every vestige of military training were eliminated from the school program.
As was pointed out to me in the debate in Montreal, the report of this committee was not agreeable, and a second committee was sent out which came in and made an opposite report. This looks to me as though it seemed very important to certain people that military training should not be discredited in the minds of the people of Canada.
There are many countries that have thrown over military training for schoolboys, after a trial of some ten or fifteen years, believing that it was not good for the boys either physically or mentally. France is one of the outstanding examples of this.
	.
I have always contended, and I feel I am right in saying that constant military training does something to the mind of the growing youth. It is not only that his body is trained into military actions, but his mind becomes a military mind, although he may be unconscious of it. When the time comes for a decision to be made as to how a national or international situation should be solved, people who have been trained along military lines quite naturally-I am certainly not blaming them-think of this particular method of settling disputes. I think enough was said the other day on the general subject of military training as a method of settling disputes, and it need not be gone into again. Even the daily newspapers are seeing that it is time we found some new way of settling disputes, and an editorial in the Toronto Daily Star of November 11, 1927, said:
Every reasoning creature must perceive that the true interests of the race are bound up in the efforts of those who seek to organize internationally against the recurrence of war and for the stamping out of such small outbreaks of it as cannot be foreseen and prevented.
I could go on and on but I do not wish to keep an impatient house. I could quote from prominent world authorities and splendid writers wiho agree that if war served a purpose for humanity at one time it is now finished, and it is time we found some other way of settling our disputes. But if our Department of National Defence is going to take the boys in our schools throughout Canada, more and more of them as the years go by, and train them to this one way of settling disputes, how in the -world are we going to find any other way? It is for that reason that I am so strongly opposed to this particular vote. Other parts of the militan' estimates are not agreeable to me; .there are many people in Canada to whom they are agreeable, but I think the majority of the people in Canada are against this vote. I believe that if we could get their opinion on the matter they would ask the government to keep their hands off the schools. Let them work through any other agency they like, work with people who are full grown and who can make their own judgments. Children are not always in position to do this, and I think it is utterly unfair to use them, because that is what we are doing, and to make them only instruments in the hands of people who want to keep on settling international disputes by the method known as war.
I will not speak at any greater length for the moment, but before sitting down I would

like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) :
That item 85 be reduced by the sum of $499, 999.

I would like to indicate
to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) that I am not impatient at all She has a perfect right, and those whom she represents have a perfect right to express their views, and I want to meet them if I can. The hon. member has expressed herself with regard to a number of matters which have already been discussed, but there is just one point I want to mention. She has an idea that the cadet training, the physical training, or whatever is done in the schools, has some sort of bad effect on tile mentality of the boys who undergo it. I want to point out to her only this, and it seems to me it is a complete answer to all that is said along that line-if military training is such that it teaches girls, boys and young men always to go into a military life and to become militaristic, that is to put military things and the militaristic spirit above the ordinary things of commercial and social life, how is it that of the boys who go through the Royal Military college at Kingston and who there get as complete a training as young men can in military matters while they are in the formative stage in life, something less than ten per -cent go into military life, while the rest of them go into business, commerce, the arts and sciences and all the other occupations which go to make up our nation's activities? It is also found, however, that when the time comes that the country must defend itself, these same young men are equipped and ready and above eighty-five per -cent of the men who went through the Royal Military college went overseas in the- great war. That assists me in coming to a conclusion and it ought to convince my hon. friends and others who have an idea that military training creates a military mentality. The situation is quite the reverse. It teaches these young men to be good citizens; that there is something to live for in this country; that while we talk about our natural resources, our opportunities and the many things which are good in Canadian life, those things are good enough to defend and when the call comes, they are ready to defend them. If my hon. friend will look up the records of many men not only in this country but in England as well, she will find that the strongest advocates of peace have had their share of military training and on that account they have not had their peaceful instincts stultified, but they have been ready all the more to advocate peace,
Supply-National Defence
just as the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Adshead) suggests, because they have had the experience of military training and they know something about the seriousness of war.

Will the minister make it ciear that this question of cadet training is perfectly optional, first, by the provinces, second, by the schools and, lastly, by the parents themselves? Has Alberta asked the government for military training in that province? I rather think it has. Another point 1 took up with the Minister of National Defence last year was this. Some complaints were sent in that in a school where a military gentleman was training the scholars, those who did not see fit to take military training were ridiculed, held up to scorn by the military officer. I could not substantiate that myself, although there was some evidence in that respect, but I should like the minister to give his opinion, so that it may go on Hansajrd, that military training is quite optional just in the same way as a scholar can choose between taking up science or languages, and that a boy will not be taunted because he does not choose military training any more than if he chooses to take up science in place of languages.

I have before me the application for cadet corps, and I can assure my hon. f-riend that the roll which is sen-t forward with the application contains the signatures of boys who desire to go into the corps, and that it is certified to- be signed with the approval of the parents or guardians. In the second place the application itself is to be signed by the minister or superintendent of education of the province or by the chairman of the board of education. Third, with regard to Alberta, I have under my hand the agreement with regard to that province just as I have the agreements with regard to the other provinces. Fourth, with regard to the matter of any scorn or ridicule or anything of that sort, I can assure my hon. friend, as I assured him at the time, that if such is the case it is absolutely contrary to instructions and ordere. I would be only too glad if he wo-uld give -me any instance in which that occurs and I would see ^ that it was followed up -and that disciplinary action was taken.
Amendment (Miss Macphail) negatived.

arsenal at Quebec. There is a small amount of some $9,000 for care of an arsenal which was established at Lindsay during the war. That is still being retained but it is not being operated.

Does the minister not think in the interest of Canada the department should be manufacturing poison gases? What good are rifles going to be against poison gas? Is Canada not getting some poison gas ready?

My hon. friend the other

endeavouring not to attempt experimental Work but to carry on with the fundamentals in connection with military training. The matter of gas is not engaging the attention of the department at all, except that I think we have on hand one or two thousand gas respirators which we use for anti-gas training.

Is it possible for the public
to secure any of these Ross rifles for sporting purposes?
No. I have been approched a great many times in regard to that.

Item agreed to.
Non-permanent active militia, $2,315,000.

What is the explanation
of the increase?

I dealt with this briefly
the other night. The increase in the estimate is to provide for an average of twelve days training at camp. Previous to the war, the average number of days training was sixteen days. Nine days training hardly provides one week at camp. Not very much can be done on the first day and the last day and you have not much left in the way of training for officers; so it was suggested-and I think it is in the interests of economy, and will result in better training, and in the long run save money-that we should provide for a greater number of days at camp. As the committee may know, the city units train largely at local headquarters. Perhaps they have three or four days at camp, and the rest of the training at local headquarters. This is more for rural units than for city units.

In view of the new
methods of warfare that are likely to prevail in any future wars, does the minister really think that this militia training is of any value at all, even against invasion?

The principles of infantry and artillery training I think are just as sound now as they ever were. My hon. friend will find that the advance and the change which is being made in connection with training both in England and the United States is largely along the line of the mechanization of transport, but you have to have artillery

Supply-National Dejence
training just the same, no matter how you haul the gun, whether by horse, motor, or some special tractor devise. Of course tanks are being experimented with, at very great expense, and as my hon. friend knows, the tanks were an invention of the last war. I do think that all we can hope to do is to train along fundamental lines so far as infantry, artillery and cavalry training is concerned, and then be prepared, if such an untoward event should come about that we are at war, to utilize the specialists in connection with tank warfare and mechanization and things of that kind; because the last war showed us that if people understand the fundamentals they can pretty easily adapt themselves to the new species of transport and the new species of armament. .
How many men will be in training at camp this year.

The whole training will
be about 33,000.

How does
that compare with last year?
It is the same.

In view of our new status as a nation, it does not seem surprising that the militia estimates should be increased. When the leader of the Progressive party spoke regarding our protection in case of future wars, I thought possibly the government would take into consideration the splendid showing made by Canadians in the last war as air pilots. Canada supplied practically 60 per cent of the air pilots overseas, and I thought possibly the government would be making some provision for the development of an aerial service because of the part that air forces will play in future wars. It is rather surprising that at the present time we have practically no aerodromes, and no provision made in that respect. All of us know the part played _ by aeroplanes in the last war, and as I said before, the Canadians excelled as air pilots.
It is rather amusing to hear the different speeches in this house regarding war. We listen patiently to hon. members speaking of war, but when did Canada ever become a warlike nation? We have never entered into a war unless it was practically forced1 upon us, and yet members rise in the house and make these long orations. The hon. member for West Calgary congratulates the government for being a peaceful government, and the hon. member for Southeast Grey accuses the government of spending great amounts
on military training and of being a warlike government. I would suggest that the great peace advocates in this house should have a conference among themselves and determine what is the actual status of the government in regard to war, and what is the great cause of these periodical outbursts on the subject of peace.

Some who care for military life take commissions in the imperial army, but I do not think that proves they are the most proficient.

But I was wondering whether it is a good thing to spend this enormous sum in educating these boys and then have a number of them-we will not say whether they are the most proficient or not- go over to the old land to find a career.

If there was a very large number out of the total enrollment I presume my hon, friend's objection might hold, but from the point of view of Canada I do not think there can be any objection with respect to the few who take imperial commissions. Ninety per cent of these boys enter civilian life and do not follow a military career.

Have the students of
the Royal Military college any more advantages in the way of lower railway fares or free equipment than the students in any other college throughout Canada? If so, what are they?
As was said, they put up what amounts to something like $400 a year.
But do they pay their railway fares to and from home?

Coming to the school to enroll and returning home When they graduate
they are given their railway fare.
And are the horses and uniforms provided by the state?

Yes.

Supply-National Defence
Rather generous, don't you think?
They pay for their uniforms. The horses are provided for the students.

In corresponding institutions
in the United States the student pays nothing; he is paid.

I do not care what they do in the United States. The only fair comparison to make is between students in other colleges of Canada and those at the Royal Military college. Because they do more in other countries to encourage the military training of boys is no justification for doing it here.

I do not think my hon. friend gives sufficient consideration to the fact that the Royal Military college is open to every Canadian boy, no matter whether he is rich or poor. As was very properly said soon after the opening of this session: merit counts; a boy gets in on merit alone.

There is a little
more to be considered in connection with the military college than has been brought out. Every cadet has to be an officer after he has graduated; he has to be connected with some unit in Canada. He is on the reserve after that. At present some of them are training for the air force; five have to take a three year course each year for air force in the civilian service. In addition to that there is also provided what is known as the long course training for officers. That expenditure goes on the military college but it is really an expenditure in connection with staff work. As regards the imperial army, there is an opening there for the very beat engineers in the world, and every Canadian is proud of the position held by Girouard in South Africa, who was the principal officer there, he having made possible all the bridge work. These men are not always looking after military work; railways and other undertakings are under their advisement. So that in a great many ways this college is providing for the advancement of civilian life. I do not think there is any establishment that has advertised the name of Canada as much as this college, and I would suggest to the minister, in view of the motion pictures which are exhibited in this country, such the The Great Parade, and which are nothing but an advertisement for the school at West Point in the United States, that it would be much better for Canada to advertise its own school. These boys immediately
on graduating from military college take up scientific work in chemistry, engineering and so forth, and they carry their talent into all civilian activities in Canada. But they are the great reservist force of the Dominion.

Does the minister think it would be necessary to increase the army in order that, all men graduating from the college who wish to take up a military career may have an opportunity? Surely you should not hold down the Canadian boys who want to go in for a military career? Had you not better consider increasing the force?
I will consider the suggestion if my hon. friend tells me she will vote for it.

Royal Canadian Air Force-all expenses in connection with the general maintenance and training of the Royal Canadian Air Force, and the auxiliary and reserve air force, including training personnel for civil air operations, $1,669,694.

Will the minister make clear to the committee the position of the men serving in the Air Force? Are they entitled to pensions at the expiration of their service and are they protected in case of accident in the air? If so, what is the nature of the protection?

There are two situations to be considered, one which presents itself when the particular airman is still in the employ of the department, and the other after he is discharged. The disabilities pension act which was the subject of an amendment this session-I am referring to the Pensions Act covering the military and naval service as well-applies to airmen and others who are discharged, or to their dependents if the man dies from any cause attributable to service. They get the same pension as those who served in the permanent force. In addition to that we have under the pay and allowance regulation's, sections 298 to 308. provided for compensation and for treatment of those who have suffered injury, disease or illness arising from a cause incident to air force service. Provision has also been made with respect to those of civilian occupation in other branches of the government service who may be accompanying airmen on service. They are provided for by order in council which has been passed under the ail board legislation. They are well covered both by the Pensions Act and by the pay and allowance regulations.

M!r. WOODSWORTH: Why is it necessary to have the civil air force under the National Defence department?
One might as well question a shoemaker with regard to the advisability of cobbling shoes.

I am asking a
serious question.

My hon. friend must not take offence at the remark; I merely wished to imply that it was not fair for him to expect a disinterested answer from me because I happen to preside over the Air force as well as the Defence department. However, I will state the facts and my hon. friend may draw his own conclusion. The air services in Canada were established first under the air board and were then taken over by the Department of National Defence. At their inception they had to do particularly with military air service, but it was soon found that the aviation service could well be utilized in connection with a number of government activities. For two or three years the air force did that work. Last year the government decided that there should be a straight division between military and civil government operations and so it was that on July 1 we set up in the Department of National Defence a separate organization in this regard. Most of the personnel are still in the air force. There is a demand in Canada, which we cannot supply, for aviators, and these men are constantly being asked by commercial companies to enter their employ. I can assure my hon. friend that we are making the transition as fast as we can in an endeavour to establish a purely civilian organization. Already the department of the controller of civil aviation is under the Civil Service Commission, and positions are being filled entirely by civilian personnel.
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a serious accident that occurred the other day.
My hon. friend can take it up on the next vote.

speechtext:
No doubt the hon. gentlemen on the front benches do not like to see such an amendment brought in to an important public bill which affects the people of western Ontario. A few of the hon. gentlemen on the front benches in connection with this and other private bills are nearly "all front and bench" and no public rights-from wha-t I have heard and seen on private bills legislation in this chamber for the past month. We have asked the Minister of Railways and the government for a statement of their policy on this particular bill, which affects the territory around St. Thomas. I spoke in the St. Thomas city hall with the late Sir Adam Beck in connection with a hydro radial to run from lake Erie through St. Thomas, the counties of Perth, Elgin and Middlesex, and on to Tillsonburg. The people of St. Thomas carried the by-law at that time by ten to one, and if was also carried in Port Burwell. The late Sir Adam Beck proposed to build a system of hydro radials in western Ontario through the counties of Middlesex
3768	COMMONS
London and Port Burwell Railway
and Elgin and other counties, which would have relieved this parliament of the cost of such a railway as this. The people carried the by-laws in every municipality. Where is the head of the national railways? He is the gentleman that has crucified the whole thousand miles of hydro radials in Toronto, London and St. Thomas and the Niagara district. Sir Adam's scheme of hydro radials would have been just as successful as his light and power scheme proved to be, and would have acted as a feeder to the whole Canadian National Railway system. I was in the county of Middlesex and the county of Elgin with my late leader, and we carried all our light and power by-laws by 100 to 1, and we carried the radial by-laws by a large majority. These radials would have acted as feeders to the main line of the Canadian National, to bring dairy products, vegetables, and agricultural products of all kinds to the main line. The light and power proposition has done wonders for the western part of Ontario, and the hydro radials would have done just as much.
Sir Adam Beck took an old railway, the Pere Marquette, he electrified it from the city of London, through St. Thomas down to Port Stanley, and this road, about 26 miles in all, has conferred a great boon on the citzens of the cities of London and St. Thomas and the other municipalities in that district. Now this bill 58 will more or less parallel the London and Port Stanley-it serves much of the same territory, which further is Canadian National exclusive territory.
A petition is presented by private people, through the medium of bill No. 58, and we must see who these people are. There is Mr. Lockrow of the city of Birmingham in the state of Michigan, attorney at law and Robert L. Harp of the city of Detroit. He will act as and will be a very happy harp for Sir Henry Thornton, the crucifier of the hydro radials. A thousand miles of road were to be 'built under Sir Adam's hydro radial scheme, representing 268 Ontario municipalities that had carried these 'bylaws, not only in the Toronto district, but in the Niagara-London, St. Thomas and Port Burwell districts. These hydro by-laws were carried, and we would have had a line from Port Burwell on the north shore of lake Erie to the city of London, St. Thomas and Listowel and Tillsonburg. Sir Henry Thornton attended the railway committee while this, bill was up and he did not oppose this bill 58, but a few years ago he opposed the hydro radial scheme, which had been passed by the ratepayers of 
the municipalities from Port Burwell, right up through St. Thomas and down to the town of Tillsonburg. It is a happy coincidence that I have here the evidence regarding as to these hydro radials, taken before the railways and shipping committee in 1924 and 1925, and Sir Henry was asked why he opposed the hydro radials. He sent a wire to Toronto opposing the' hydro radials and said he wanted the entire territory and would electrify the Grand Trunk line to the falls, to Montreal and elsewhere, which was never done.
The people in these municipalities have put up their bonds to build these hydro radials in the counties of Elgin and Middlesex, to build the London and Port Stanley Railway. These bonds have been guaranteed by the province of Ontario, and it is now proposed to make a scrap of paper out of these securities and allow a new private road to invade their territory. These people come along and say, "We will scrap all this territory; we will scrap all these bonds, and destroy the life work of Sir Adam Beck in the county of Middlesex and Elgin." Sir Adam Beck did more for the counties of Elgin and Middlesex and western Ontario than a thousand Sir Henry Thorntons.
Where was he when this bill was before the railway committee? He was asked what his views were regarding a line going through these counties, and he replied that he had no interest in this railway (Bill 58). Of course he had no interest in this railway. I can remember the time when it was estimated that a third of a million dollars was put up to defeat Sir Adam Beck and hydro radials in Toronto by the electric ring. I was with my late leader in the counties of Elgin and Middlesex when we launched the investment of the municipalities in the London and Port Stanley Railway. It is a fine road and a shining example of what the public ownership of radials would have done for the people generally in radials all over the province of Ontario. I regret to say that my late leader was driven to the wall, and some of these American corporations have found western Ontario now a very happy hunting ground now owing to the fact that we have as head of the National railways a gentleman who does not believe in public ownership. This man has fought hydro radial by-laws in the city of Toronto, and in the counties of Elgin and Middlesex, in season and out of season, and helped destroy the hydro radials. He says he is not interested in these radial by-laws. Of course he is not interested in the radial by-laws; he is only giving them

London and Port Burwell Railway
the same kind of bunkum which he gave to the taxpayers in Toronto by wire during the radial election. Sir Henry Thornton was asked in the committee on railways and shipping what his hostility was to the scheme of Sir Adam Beck to build a thousand miles of hydro radials in the province of Ontario. He was asked what his views were, and he said that if he had to do it over again he would never have sent the telegram he did on the eve of I he presentment of the hydro radial by-law to the taxpayers of Toronto.
We have to go back to history to get the chronological order of this thing. The hydro by-law was defeated in the city of Toronto, and we can see to-day in Michigan, New York, New Jersey and Indiana what a system of hydro radials has done there, and would have done here for the counties of Elgin and Middlesex and western part of Ontario if adopted. Many of these cities and towns are suffering from rural depopulation. There is under-production; the farmers are not able to get their crops to the market and in many cases farm produce is suffering from lack of transportation. In many counties farms are untilled. Why? Because of lack of transportation facilities and the lack of electric hydro radials.
Sir Adam Beck, in addressing the people of the district covered by Bill No. 58, pointed out that if we had a system of hydro radials built by the municipalities it would solve the great problem of under-production in Ontario. He told them that they would haul the farmer's crop to the market; that they would multiply the value of every farm in Middlesex, Elgin and other Ontario counties by two, three or four, as has been done in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio, New York and New Jersey. What built up these five states across the border? Their system of hydro radials. When Sir Henry Thornton took over the presidency of the Canadian National, by-laws had been passed in the various municipalities approving the hydro radial system. I was over the whole right of way of this particular road and every bylaw was carried. I cannot speak for Tillson-burg, because I do not remember the by-law there, but I remember being in the county of Elgin and the city of St. Thomas. This is one of the many contracts between the entire 262 municipalities. Port Burwell, the city of St. Thomas, the city of London, and the town of TiHsonburg are in the contract. These contracts passed the ratepayers. The bydaw was prepared by the municipalities; it was endorsed by the hydro-electric commission; it was sent to the people and on municipal voting day the ballot boxes were opened. Those who were ratepayers in these municipalities of western Ontario which enjoy cheap light and power went into the polls and by large majorities all the municipalities covered by this particular bill 58 preferred a hydro radial system, acting as a feeder for the old Grand Trunk, affiliated and connected with it. Many of these municipalities to-day, only for the work of Sir Henry Thornton, would be linked up with the London and Port Stanley railway, and with the great hydro trunk line between Toronto, Hamilton and the city of Windsor, with this particular right of way along the north shore of lake Erie and all the branch lines operating in western Ontario as a net work conneoting up in western Ontario the rural municipalities, the suburban municipalities and the urban municipalities and by a vast trunk line extending over to Niagara Falls, St. Catharines, Hamilton and Toronto and not by duplication but taking existing old Grand Trunk dilapidated lines in western Ontario and electrifying them and acting as part and parcel of the old Grand Trunk.
These by-laws in the various municipalities were carried under Sir Adam Beck's auspices, some of them by a hundred to one, some by ten to one, some by five to one and some by three to one. Everything was going along lovely for the adoption of a system of hydro radials in western Ontario and in the Niagara district around lake Erie and lake Ontario, when like a bolt out the blue there descended upon those municipalities a gentleman by the name of Sir Henry Thornton, who is supposed to be president of the Canadian National. The municipalities were to construct these railways themselves, or take over old dilapidated Grand Trunk lines; they were to act as feeders for the old bankrupt Grand Trunk in western Ontario. This question was discussed in the house the oither night by the Minister of Railways, and I have a great respect for him. I differ with him now; I will differ with him many times in the future, but I know that he is sincere in his belief. I have always found him sincere in what he says, but I have not found the same sincerity in regard to the president of the Canadian National. He fought Sir Adam Beck in season and out of season. When this hydro radial by-law was brought up in Toronto he sent a wire to the minister stating that he was going to electrify the whole Grand Trunk from Toronto to Montreal; that he was going to electrify the road which passes through the municipalities from Toronto to Niagara Falls. Another line to be electrified was from Toronto to Barrie and another was the Toronto and Eastern railway from Leaside down to the town of Bowmanville. Now I find that the

whole Toronto and Eastern railway has been tom up by Sir Henry Thornton. I had a return brought down in the house and it showed that the Toronto and Eastern railway, which would have been a hydro radial from Toronto to Bowmanville and Cobourg, a railway which Sir Adam Beak was to electrify was torn up. Sir Henry Thornton did the same thing with the contract for the purchase of the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto railway which Sir Adam had a contract to purchase. He cancelled it and he did the same thing with the Toronto suburban railway running through the Humber valley to the city of 'Guelph. These three railways belonging to a bankrupt road were to be taken over 'by Sir Adam Beck and the municipalities passed by-laws by a large majority for their acquisition. What happened? After the present government came into office they cancelled the orders in council of the late government and declined to give the hydro radials these three railways which would have been developed and extended under public ownership as free feeders for the Canadian National and have saved the people of Canada all the cost of betterments now spent on these systems.
The Toronto and Eastern railways, for example, which would have acted as a feeder, has been torn up by Sir Henry Thornton. As you pass out of the village of Leaside, what do you see? You see ties torn up, bridges tom up, right of way torn up. Would that we bad on both sides of this house some public-spirited men like my leader, Sir Adam Beck, who was the 'best Conservative we ever had in the province and who was a voting strength to the Conservative party. When the ballot boxes were opened in the municipalities it was found that they gave big majorities to the hydro radial system proposed by Sir Adam Beck.
We have to-day a gentleman who comes to this house and promotes this bill and I charge in the house that these two United States citizens who are connected with this bill are nothing but dummies for the National railways. Some of Sir Henry Thornton's officials were connected with a bridge bill the other day here-a bridge engineer and Grand Trunk Railways brakeman and one of his officials on the railway promoting a bill. To-night this bill is being promoted by a gentleman from Birmingham in the United States of America. He is an attorney-at-law. Of course he is an attomey-at-law. One of the duties of an attorney is to be at law.
[Mr. Church.)
There is another gentleman from Detroit, called Robert Lee Harp. That is a nice-sounding name. He is playing the harp, but the chief harper and the chief fiddler who defeated the hydro radials and to put this bill through is Sir Henry Thornton, the one who destroyed Sir Adam Beck's whole dream of radiaJs in Ontario. There are papers in my own city and in many other parts of the province which have fought for Sir Adam Beck in season and out of season.

speechtext:
I will, although it is pretty hard, Mr. Speaker, to separate the question of the public Ontario hydro radials from the private bill that is now before us. The territory that is to be covered by the London and Port Burwell Railway Company and this bill is and was hydro radial territory. At the present time the London and Port Stanley Railway Company have this territory in agreement with the county councils of Elgin and Middlesex counties. These are the two counties mainly concerned, except for a small portion of the county of Perth through which this road is to go. I have already dealt with the question of the territory to be served.
Now I come to discuss this proposed line of railway, which in my opinion would parallel the London and Port Stanley road. If I remember rightly, the county council of the county of Elgin and Perth asked to have the hydro radial system extended into these counties. By this bill we would wipe out the London and Port Stanley railway, and launch on this new line of railway. Bill No. 58 received its first reading on March the 6th, and has already been reported. I am moving the six months' hoist, Mr. Speaker, for the reason that I am attacking this bill on grounds of public policy. In the second place, I attack it because this road would invade Canadian National territory which never should be surrendered. The Canadian National railway has already a large deficit, and it is going behind about $8,000,000 in its passenger business, and I say that it should

London and Port Burwell Railway
not give up territory which would serve as a feeder to its main line. This proposed line of railway runs through the counties of Middlesex and Elgin, and virtually parallels the London and Port Stanley road, and if this bill goes through, the London and Port Stanley road might as well close up. For these reasons I think the bill should not be adopted by this house. It is opposed to the rights of the municipalities. The city of St. Thomas is already tied up to a contract with the London and Port Stanley railway, and if this bill goes through it will finish somewhat that contract. The Ontario Hydro Electric Commission has bonds running into the hundreds and thousands of dollars of these various municipalities, and if this bill goes through it would destroy somewhat those securities. It is something that has never been done before.
Who are the Canadians that are connected with this proposed line of railway? They are John H. Teall, gentleman, Donald F. Gibson, barrister-at-law, Frederick A. Ramsay, merchant, all of the town of Tillsonfourg. To please my hon. friend the chairman of the banking and commerce committee, who is in favour of this bill, and for whom I have the utmost regard, as I have also for the promoter of this bill, and for the hon. member from Elgin too, I might be inclined to support the bill, but as a supporter of the Ontario hydro radial system, I cannot do it. I know that these people in the municipalities concerned are behind the scheme of Sir Adam Beck, and I cannot, surrender the views 1 hold after having been connected with the Ontario hydro radial system for twenty-two years.
This work is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, but not by the widest stretch of the imagination can it be called that. The road is not interprovincial in character; it is not international; it is simply a small provincial railway, which would parallel the London and Port Stanley road, and a federal railway in a mythical sense only.
I understand that an amendment is to be moved in regard to what the capital shall be. They are to issue preferred stock apparently. The head office of the company is to be in the town of Port Burwell, in the county of Elgin, and the annual meeting of the shareholders is to be held on the first Monday of October. It is provided that the number of directors is to be not less than five nor more than nine, and that the company may lay out, construct and operate a railway from Port Burwell on the north shore of lake Erie
to the city of London, passing through the counties of Elgin and Middlesex. For these and other reasons, Mr. Speaker, I move that this bill be not now read a third time, but that it be read a third time this day six months.

how Port Burwell is already served by the Canadian Pacific Railway, that there is not enough business to keep one road busy, so that without a great influx of population, of which there is no immediate prospect, two roads could not possibly be successful.
In regard to no influx of population, I have looked up the census of Canada for 1921, and I find that the population in the district is less than it was in 1901. Those census figures deal with four townships and three villages. The townships are Malahide, Bayham, Yarmouth and South Dorchester. In 1901 the township of Malahide had a population of 3,795; in 1921, 3,191. In 1901 the township of Bayham had a population of 3,771; in 1921, 3,438. In 1901 the township of Yarmouth had a population of 5,089; in 1921, 5,212. In 1901 the township of South Dorchester had a population of 1,637; in 1921, 1,550. Taking the four townships together there were 900 fewer people in that district in 1921 than in 1901. The villages comprise Aylmer, Springfield and Vienna. In 1901 Aylmer had a population of 2,204; in 1921, 2,194. In 1901 Springfield had a population of 501; in 1921, 460. In 1901 Vienna had a population of 352; in 1921, 288. So that there were 115 fewer people in these three towns or villages in 1921 than in 1901. Taking the whole district together, the population has diminished by about one thousand. But it is curious that the town of Port Stanley and the city of St. Thomas, which are not touched by this proposed railway, have gained in population in the decades I have mentioned. In 1901 Port Stanley had a population of 552; in 1921, 973. In 1901 St. Thomas had a population of 11,485; in 1921, 16,026. In other wordis, Port Stanley and St. Thomas have increased considerably in population since 1901. In view of these figures and the fact that there is no general demand for more railways, I submit that the facilities in that area are adequate. I wish to bring to the attention of the house another feature, and that is the relative mileage of the London and Port Stanley Railway and of the proposed road. ' The London and Port
Stanley Railway is twenty-four miles long while the proposed line is thirty-four miles, according to the sponsor of the bill. That is to say, it has 40 per cent more trackage. It has ten miles more of right of way to purchase. On that account it will have a higher cost of construction, a higher cost for interest and sinking fund, and a higher cost for maintenance and operation. To balance that the freight rate is being considered. Some people have the idea that the installation of the road will result in lower freight rates on coal and coke from Erie to London. I would point out that the freight rates are fixed by the Railway Commissioners, the rate from Port Stanley to London being the governing rate. That is the established rate, and all other lines which find their way to London will have to charge rates correspondingly. These rates, I say, are fixed and confirmed by the railway commission.
It is said by the promoters of the bill that the success of the railroad depends on the success of the coking plant Which it is proposed to establish. Central Canada is of course very much interested in fuel to replace anthracite coal. All our supplies of anthracite come from the United States. These supplies of coal are being depleted and before long central Canada will have to find an additional supply of fuel. We have been trying out substitutes and have used small shipments of Alberta coal. Many people have turned to coke and a number of others to the use of oil. Now the matter of establishing a coking plant is a very important one, but I do not intend at the present moment to go into the pros and cons of coke production. My information is that the proposed amount which is to be spent on the coking plant is utterly inadequate for the installation which will be required to establish a going concern which will be able to compete with others already putting goods on the market. It seems to me, from what I can gather, that it would take two or three times the amount of capital which it is proposed to spend in order to install a thoroughly equipped coking plant.
In the railway committee the promoter of the bill was asked as to the type of coking plant which it is proposed to establish. He was uncertain; he did not seem to know the difference between certain types of 'coking plants; but he did say, I think, that there were three or four kinds, any one of which might be used. At any rate he gave no particularly definite information concerning the plant. Now, I know of one firm in London who are interested in things of this kind and
3774	COMMONS
London and Port Burwell Railway
who had a great deal of engineering advice on the matter. They went into it most thoroughly and exhaustively and they came to the conclusion that the installation of a coking plant was not likely to be a paying proposition. Accordingly they abandoned the idea. It might be that in other respects this proposal would be a success, but there are many questions which ought to be considered in regard to this proposed plant and which so far have not been answered. Rather than take on the responsibilities and uncertainties of railroad operation, this company might very well turn its attention to the production of coke and gas and refuse to have anything whatever to do with the railway project. I am quite sure that the operation of the railroad will so cripple this company that the coking plant will fall by the wayside. Otherwise it might be a success. At. page 3919 of Hansard the sponsor of the bill is reported in connection with the question. Speaking in regard to the finances, he said:
This company -are not asking, nor do they intend to ask, for any assistance financially or otherwise, except that they be given the privilege to spend their money in this manner.
I ask, whose money is going to be spent? In the meeting of the railway committee when the question came up, the promoter mentioned certain hypothetical circumstances
which would prevent the railway from selling its bonds. I should judge from that statement that the company proposes to sell bonds to the public. In that case, of course, it can hardly be said that the railway company is spending its own money. It means that the public-no matter where they may be-who can be influenced to buy bonds will be the investors, and not the gentlemen who are seeking a charter for the road.
I could give several examples of losses which the people even in that section have suffered on account of activities of this kind. In my previous remarks I referred to the liquidation of the South Western Traction Company., a radial lino which ran from London to Port Stanley at one time and which had charters to run to various other towns in western Ontario. Those who invested money in that concern lost it. That was followed by the London and Lake Erie Transportation Company, which operated for a while and then followed in the footsteps of the traction company. It went into liquidation and the ruins of some of its works are to be seen to-day. The bond holders have nothing to show for their investment in that road except these ruins.

I have been treated to a little editorial comment in connection with this matter. A few days ago an editorial appeared in a newspaper, this statement being made, that London had the reputation of putting an old established firm out of business on account of its going into railroad operation. Let me say that London was operating the Port Stanley road fifty-three years before this company referred to went into business. Consequently th firm referred to, the London and Lake Erie Transportation Company, were forced to go out of business.
Parliament should study most carefully the prospects of every railroad before allowing the passage of bills which may ultimately in volve losses to the general public. This house has made some efforts to move along that direction, and the matter is covered to a great extent by a report made by the Drayton-Acworth commission.
