I have said a few words
about the previous item, and what I wish to speak of now is a very serious aeroplane accident that happened at St. Alexander, not far from Riviere du Loup, on Saturday last.
I shall be very brief, but I wish to give our friends of the press gallery a scoop. It was not mentioned in the papers, but an aeroplane belonging to the Transcontinental Airways, a company which has a contract with the Post Office department, crashed. The aeroplane left Montreal for Rimouski, where
there is a landing field, but on account of the foggy weather the pilot was unable ta land. He could not see the field, and he had to go back to Quebec. As his supply of gas was nearly exhausted he tried to land near Riviere du Loup, an important city, just about halfway between Rimouski and Quebec. There is no landing field there, the country being all divided up by fences and ditches, and it was not possible for him to find a suitable landing place, although he flew very low and tried to locate a favourable spot. Not succeeding, he went- further on his way to Quebec, and at St. Alexander, as his supply of gas was very low, he had to come down, and his machine was wrecked in landing. Fortunately, he was not hurt. My point, Mr. Chairman, is that in the United States, in Mexico and in other countries with air routes there are landing fields. Hydroplanes have been used experimentally, but owing to the conditions at certain times on the St. Lawrence river they were not found satisfactory; aeroplanes are now used rather exclusively, especially along the St. Lawrence river. The distance from Montreal to Rimouski is about 375 miles, and I desire to ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) if he intends to build a landing field at Riviere du Loup. Such a field would be a real help for aviators and would improve the mail service over that route. Riviere du Loup is an ideal location, being not not very far from New Brunswick and Maine; in fact, it is one of the best sites in eastern Quebec for such a purpose. Does fhe department buy the ground or does it help the local authorities to acquire the necessary site? Also, does the department erect any buildings on landing fields?

I may say that the department- has not under consideration the provision of a landing field at the point mentioned. My hon. friend may not know that the company to which he refers, Transcontinental Airways Limited, has the contract for carrying the mails from Montreal to Rimouski, and under that contract the company must itself provide any intermediate landing fields. It is impossible for the department to forecast the need for landing fields along the route. While a fog settled over the point which my hon. friend mentioned, forcing the plane to land, on another occasion the forced landing might be somewhere where it would be impracticable to provide a field. Therefore the contractor has to provide his own facilities at intermediate points.



Supply-National Defence
The general policy of the department is not to provide landing fields except solely for government services. We are endeavouring to encourage municipalities all over the country to realize the importance to their own towns of themselves providing these facilities. On request the department sends a qualified officer to look over the proposed site and to advise on the preparation of the landing field.
Does the department contribute towards providing such fields or for their maintenance?

No. The only contribution the department makes is to send officers to advise on suitable sites and for their preparation for aviation purposes. This is generally the system in the United States where they have many municipal aerodromes.

Somehow or other it is commonly accepted ;n Canada that the matter of public health s assigned by statute to the provinces. We who have studied this question have submitted that point to legal authorities, some of whom say that we are not working along national lines in connection with the public health of our country. It is held by some that the maj or matters of public health should be looked after by the parliament of Canada.
The only matter specifically mentioned in the British North America Act in regard to public health is that of quarantine, and that matter is assigned to the federal government. Nothing is said of other matters in regard to public health, for the simple reason that in 1867 the health of the nation was really a matter which was not considered at all. We must remember that only in 1882 was an organization known as the provincial board of health started by the province of Ontario. We think to-day that if the British North America Act were to come into existence now, a great many matters which are handled at present by the provinces would be taken over by the Dominion government. The authorities state that matters which are not mentioned as specifically assigned to the provinces should be assigned to the Dominion.
Twenty-five years ago a child born in Canada had a chance to live to be thirty-three years of age, then the average life of man. Owing to the application of health principles throughout the various parts of Canada and the United States, Dr. Mayo was enabled to say in the city of Toronto about a month ago that the average span of life has been increased to fifty-eight years. This marvellous result has come about by the proper application of principles well understood to-day, and these matters are being merged and brought forward as a national effort.
I contend that the Dominion government should divide this country into certain areas. In the maritime provinces there should be about three in each province; in Quebec about ten; in Ontario ten or twelve, and so on from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The Dominion government should pay at least one-half the cost of employing permanent medical officers to supervise certain of the matters in connection with the public health of the country. If the government of Canada were to take hold of certain of the work in regard to public health and spread it over this Dominion of Canada, we would be in step with other countries and could expect to make the average life of man seventy years within fifteen years' time.
The question is so important and permeates into so many quarters that a conference should take place. Some of our leading experts on public health are to-day urging us to bring this question up in parliament, in order that what we hope will take place may be accomplished. Nothing can be done now, but I hope that a resolution will be submitted to parliament within the next few years dealing with this matter of prime importance.
